speakeroldname: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State):
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER TO INQUIRE INTO LICENSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to lay on the table copy of an order in council dated March 22, 1935, P.C. 738. This order appoints His Honour Judge James Parker, senior judge of the county court of York, in the province of Ontario, as commissioner under part 1 of the Inquiries Act, pursuant to the provisions of section 10 of the Copyright Amendment Act, to investigate and report:
(a)	Whether the Canadian Performing Right Society Limited or any other society, association or company unduly withholds the issue or grant of licences for or in respect of the performance of dramatico-musical or musical works in Canada;
(b)	Whether the Canadian Performing Right Society Limited or any other society, association or company proposes to collect excessive fees, charges or royalties in compensation for the issue or grant of such licences;
(e) Whether the Canadian Performing Right Society Limited or any other society, association or company otherwise conducts its operations in Canada in a manner which is deemed detrimental to the interests of the public.
The commissioner is also specially authorized and required to investigate and report on the fees, charges or royalties which the Canadian Performing Right Society Limited, or any such other society, association or company, should be entitled to collect from licensees in compensation for the issue or grant of such licences, and the bases on which 92582-1291
such fees, charges or royalties should properly be computed.
This order in council has been passed in compliance with the request of a large number of members on both sides of the house who have insisted that there should be an inquiry into the operations of the Canadian Performing Right Society and its associates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BANK OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this question cannot accurately be answered in its present form because in putting it my hon. friend apparently has assumed that it was competent for the banks to retain a portion of their gold, whereas if he will look at section 28 of the Bank of Canada Act he will find that the banks have to transfer the whole of their gold.
There is the further question as to that portion which should be allocated as against their foreign liabilities, and that question cannot properly be answered until the governor in council has taken action with respect to the valuation and allocation of profits.
If it meets with my hon. friend's approval I would suggest that he drop the question and put it in a revised form.

HUDSON BAY INSURANCE RATES On the orders of the day:

During the last year or two the government has been doing everything
possible to get the insurance rates reduced in connection with Hudson bay voyages. After spending such a lot of money on the building of the Hudson Bay railway we are all very anxious that it should be used as much as possible, and one of the ways in which we hope to bring that about is to endeavour to get insurance rates reduced. If the house will permit me I will read a dispatch which has been received in regard to this question:
A cable dispatch received from the High Commissioner for Canada in Great Britain on Hudson bay marine insurance rates indicates that "the joint Hull committee has agreed with the imperial shipping committee to recommend to underwriters in London and Liverpool that for the season 1935 there shall be for well found ships a reduction of 25 per cent on 1934 minimum additional premium for suspending the warrant. Vessels equipped with a gyro compass may be allowed 25 per cent off that part of the new additional premium which is calculated on insured value of ship. The dates of opening and closing of season will remain unaltered, but surcharge of 25 per cent for leaving Churchill after 7th but before October 15, being calculated on new rates of additional premium, will represent a corresponding reduction. The full report of the imperial shipping committee will be presented to the governments concerned.
I may add that the insurance rates in a case of this kind are based on actual facts; that is, they have to wait a few years to see what losses there are in order to arrive at their rates. One of the difficulties in connection with Hudson bay insurance rates is that the number of vessels going there is very small and therefore the risk at Lloyds or elsewhere is not spread over as many vessels as it would be in other parts of the ocean. But I think I am safe in saying that this concession will be greatly appreciated and will help to increase shipments from Hudson bay.

subtopic: BILL TO LIMIT HOURS OF WORK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
The question of jurisdiction has been argued many times and I do not want to say a word about it to-day except that I would like to place on Hansard an order in council just for the purpose of making complete the record on this question. This is P.C. 2325, an order in council concerning a draft convention limiting the hours of work in coal mines, adopted on October 26, 1932, and I would like to draw the attention of the house to the fact that this order in council was passed a year after the judgment in the radio case and eight months after the judgment in the aviation case. The order reads:
The committee of the privy council have had before them a report, dated 13th October, 1932, from the Minister of Justice, submitting that he has had under consideration, upon reference from the Department of Labour, the authentic text of the draft convention limiting hours of work in coal mines, adopted by the international labour conference at its fifteenth session (28th May-18th June, 1931), with a view to determining whether and to what extent the subject matter of this draft convention lies with the competence of parliament or of the provincial legislatures, in order that the said draft convention may be brought by the dominion government, in discharge of its obligation under article 405 of the treaty of Versailles and' the corresponding article of the other treaties of

peace, before the authority or authorities within whose competence the matter lies, for legislative or other action.
The minister-
That is the Minister of Justice.
-observes that the draft convention embodies various provisions with regard to the regulation of hours of work of workers employed in coal mines, that is to say, in any mine from which hard coal or lignite, or principally hard coal or lignite together with other minerals, is extracted. It contemplates that such provisions shall be given compulsory effect against the management of every mine to which such provisions are to be respectively made applicable. Ratification of the convention would consequently involve an obligation on the part of each government concerned to give effect to the provisions of the convention by legislative action in so far as existing laws may not afford adequate authority for that purpose.
The provisions of the convention which require legislative action to make them effective clearly involve legislation which, in its subject matter, would be directly concerned with classes of subjects assigned exclusively to the provincial legislatures by section 92 of the British North America Act, 1867: in particular "local works and undertakings" (section 92 (10)); "property and civil rights in the province" (section 92 (13)) and' perhaps also "generally all matters of a merely local or private nature in the province" (section 92 (16)). While legislation upon the subject matter of the provisions of the convention might perhaps be enacted by the parliament of Canada in an ancillary or incidental way in relation to any coal mine which has been declared to be a work for the general advantage of Canada: (section 91 and section 92	(10)	(c), British North America Act,
1867); Union Colliery Company of British Columbia versus Bryden (1899), A.C. 580, 585, the Minister of Justice is of opinion that legislative jurisdiction touching that subject matter is. as regards those parts of Canada included within the several provinces, primarily vested in the provincial legislatures and that it is within the competence of the several provincial governments by appropriate legislative action to give effect to the proposals of the convention generally and comprehensively, except for those parts of Canada which are not included within the limits of any province. As to the latter, exclusive legislative jurisdiction in relation to the subject matter of the convention is vested in the parliament of Canada. The minister observes that the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in the matter of legislative jurisdiction over hours of labour (1925) S.C.R. 505. affords strong support for the opinion above expressed.
The committee-
That is the whole government.
-concur in the foregoing and advise that a copy hereof, together with an authenticated copy of the draft convention, be transmitted to the lieutenant-governors of the respective provinces for the consideration of their respective governments with a view to the enactment of legislation or such other action upon the

Eight Hour Day-Mr. Heaps
subject matter of the draft convention, within the provincial sphere of jurisdiction, as each government may be advised to take.
All of which is respectfully submitted for Your Excellency's approval.
E. J. Lemaire,
Clerk of the Privy Council.
I wish only to say that the law in 1932 is still the law in 1935.

speechtext: Just a word in reply to my hon. friend's statement. In my opinion the statement of law as set forth in the order in council just read is correct, but the situation is not the same to-day as it was then. The situation to-day is that this house has approved a convention submitted under the provisions of the treaty of Versailles and we have undertaken new responsibilities under the terms of that treaty. The opinion expressed in the order in council was correct, but the convention having been approved by parliament, the whole situation is changed, and I submit that parliament now has jurisdiction.

speechtext:
I have no doubt that the constitutional point raised by the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) is a very important one to those people who are versed in constitutional law; possibly to them it may be an all-important question, but apart from that aspect of the question, there is another and more important feature involved, and that is the principle of the measure itself now before parliament. I believe the people who are to-day interested in the question of the shorter work week are ever so much more numerous than those who are interested in the constitutional aspect. I realize however on the one hand that the latter part of the question must be settled before parliament can effectively legislate along the lines as proposed in this bill; but I am satisfied on the other that the government with its legal advisers and the number of lawyers who happen to be members of the government would not have undertaken the step they did unless they felt they were justified from a legal standpoint in so doing.
The purpose I have in rising to-day is not to deal with the constitutional aspect because even if I wanted to, I could not do so. After all very often in matters of this kind the constitutional question is only relative, because our constitution changes with the needs of the times. That, I believe, is the history of the British constitution. What may
have been illegal forty or fifty years age may to-day be legal, without any change in the statutes of the country. On this occasion the government have thought fit to introduce a bill to establish in Canada a forty-eight hour working week. As far as the bill itself is concerned I do not regard it as a very important measure, but I regard the reeogpition of the principle of a maximum working week as of considerable importance. For that reason I am supporting the measure, and I am pleased indeed to see the government taking this step, even though it is so many years since the signing of the Versailles treaty. On previous occasions when I have spoken on labour problems in this house I have said that I attach more importance to legislation concerning hours of work than to some of the other legislation introduced here. We are confronted to-day with a very grave unemployment situation. Vast numbers of our citizens, men and women, are unable to find means of livelihood. I have contended in the house year in and year out, that one of the first steps we should take in order to absorb these people into industry is a considerable reduction in the hours of labour. That is why when the unemployment insurance bill was before the house I claimed that in itself it was no remedy for unemployment and could hardly be called a palliative. But now that we have this measure before us dealing with hours of labour. I hope that it will be much more far reaching in its effect than merely restricting working hours to forty-eight per week, otherwise it will not be of much more importance than the unemployment insurance measure.
I want to go back to a little over a year ago. On February 5, 1934, this house passed a resolution dealing with the shorter working week, when I introduced the following motion:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into immediate consideration the necessity of reducing the hours of labour of those engaged in industry, and also increase the purchasing power of the masses of our people in order that they may absorb the goods produced, thereby creating a more equitable distribution of our wealth production.
On that occasion the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) accepted the resolution on behalf of the government, and that motion carried unanimously. It asked for a reduction in the hours of labour and also for an increase in the purchasing power of the masses of the people. I think on that occasion I argued for a shorter working day and a thirty hour week, and this afternoon I intend
Eight Hour Day-Mr. Heaps

moving an amendment to the resolution also asking this house to approve of a thirty hour working week.
Now shorter working days in themselves of course are very important, but unless we give to the masses of the people increased purchasing power they will be very little better off with the shorter working day than at present, because it would only ipean spreading out the purchasing power now existing without increasing it to any extent. Now why have I always argued in this house and outside in favour of a shorter working week and increased purchasing power? I think it has begun to be realized that if we are going to absorb the vast number of unemployed into industry it can only be done by decreasing the hours of work, and by facilitating absorption of the goods that we are able to produce. I do not think that any one would argue that our ills to-day are due to lack of productive capacity; We have tried other remedies; for some years now we have tried public works, but even at the best public works are only a temporary palliative, they are like putting a plaster on an ulcer, covering up the sore spot but not curing the evil at its root. The question also arises whether the conditions through which we are now passing can be called abnormal. For some time it has seemed to me that these conditions which have existed for the last five years are really becoming normal. There is no person who can say that the present unfortunate conditions as to employment are not going to continue. I think we must be prepared to accept these conditions as likely to exist for some time to come in spite of all the legislation that is now before parliament. As a result of unemployment we are carrying a load which threatens to break down the financial structure of the country. The burden is becoming too great for our municipalities, our provincial governments are unable to bear it, and the federal government even cannot finance unemployment relief out of current revenue and are compelled to finance it out of borrowings or otherwise on capital account. This unemployment relief expenditure is a huge, unproductive outlay, returning nothing as far as the country is concerned, but creating untold hardship and misery. What is more important than the mere money aspect and the cost to the municipalities and the provincial and federal exchequers is the injury to the morale of the unemployed. Do we give enough attention to that? Do we think of these young boys who since leaving school 
have been unable to find any useful occupation which they may enter and take their part in the normal activities of life? Many of these young people have been out of school four or five years and have been unable to get a useful day's work. Think of the plight of the unemployed, always looking for that elusive job which cannot be found; which is something like prosperity, always around the corner. That vain search for the elusive job does more to sap the morale of many of our unemployed than anything one can imagine.
I believe on the other hand that the capitalistic system as we have it to-day cannot cure the conditions which it has created. Our economic system to-day demands on the one hand economies, and on the other huge expenditures. Our governments have been compelled to come to the assistance of many of our large financial and industrial institutions; we have been compelled to give guarantees to the banks, to give guarantees to the railways and to give guarantees to large power corporations. Yet the heads of those same institutions keep telling parliament that expenditures must be still more restricted and that the government must keep out of business. If the government did keep out of business very long these institutions would be in much worse plight than they are. Our present system compels us, in order to find employment for those out of work, to produce goods years ahead of actual requirements. Buildings have been constructed which in many cases are not required, our railway building and equipment has been in advance of our needs; that goes to indicate the chaotic condition of our economic structure at the present time, when we go on constructing things years ahead of requirements, and yet thousands of our Canadian people are compelled to go without the necessaries of life.
To-day we are living in an age of what we term contracting capitalism. Some years ago, in the middle and towards the end of the last century, we were living in an age of expanding capitalism, and as long as capitalism expanded we were able to find markets in different parts of the world for the surplus goods we produced. To-day, however, because of our tremendous productive capacity, those foreign markets are fast disappearing, and we in Canada in this connection are in exactly the same plight as are the people in other parts of the world. For instance, we supply the other parts of the world with capital goods which ultimately come into competition with the very goods

Eight Hour Day-Mr. Heaps
we produce in this country. After a time, after we have provided these so-called backward countries with articles we ourselves produce, we find that they are competitors of ours in the markets of the world, and with the increasing production in all parts of the world we have a glut of commodities on all sides with no purchasing power in the hands of the masses of the people.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that was amply recognized when we had the international labour conference at Washington in 1919. I believe that was one of the reasons which brought about that conference, at which the different nations tried by some means or other to cope with what was already, at that time, a very difficult situation, namely the over-production of commodities and the number of people even then who found themselves out of work. That was sixteen years ago, and at that time the forty-eight hour week was approved. But a great many things have happened during the past sixteen years, and I claim that in the year 1935 a forty-eight hour week or eight hour day is entirely obsolete and out of harmony with existing productive capacity. Since 1949 we have tried all kinds of remedies to meet the situation in this country. We have tried public works, relief works of one kind and another, high tariffs and many other things, but nothing has met the situation and I claim that nothing we have tried so far is able to meet the situation as it exists in the year 1935.
There have been tremendous economic changes since 1919, and one of the most important of these changes has been the vast increase in the productive capacity of the economic machine. According to a well known United States statistician, Doctor F. C. Mills, between 1919 and 1933 the productive capacity of the United States increased by 71 per cent. That was over a period of sixteen years, the exact period with which we are dealing at the present time. I would venture to assert that these figures which this eminent statistician gives in connection with the United States have been followed very closely in Canada; I think there has been a similar increase in the productive capacity of our people in Canada. Then if that is the case, Mr. Speaker, I think there should be a considerably greater reduction of hours of work, beyond forty-eight hours a week. A few weeks ago our bureau of statistics issued a bulletin to which it is well worth while to refer for a few moments. On February 7 last our statistical branch issued some figures in connection with the production of our textile industries, which I
think are of significance to us under present conditions. It is pointed out that the value of production in the cotton textile industry in 1933 was $58,451,000, an increase over the previous year of $13,110,000, or 28 per cent. In 1933 there were 17,885 persons employed in this industry, or 1,067 more than in the previous year. In 1933 the wages amounted to $13,220,000, an increase over 1932 of
S61,000,	or one-half of 1 per cent. I want the house to appreciate these figures. Though there was an increase in production of 28 per cent, in the same year there was an increase in wages of only one-half of 1 per cent. Though there were 1,067 more persons employed in 1933 than in 1932, wages increased by only one-half of 1 per cent. If those wages were divided equally among those employed I believe there would be an actual decrease in the wages paid the men and women employed in our textile industries, in spite of the fact that there was a 28 per cent increase in production.
That is simply an example of what is taking place all the time. When the government issue figures from time to time tending to show that production has been increased by so much, in textiles, in boots and shoes, in furniture and so on, it does not necessarily mean that more people have been employed. Probably it only means that the machines have been a little busier and have turned out more goods than in the previous year. That has been one of the main factors in the creation of that vast army of unemployed in Canada to-day, despite the fact that there has been a certain increase in our production in the last year or so. In this country we can always produce far more than we can reasonably consume, and in addition to our huge surplus of production we have a vast reservoir of workers anxiously awaiting the opportunity to be absorbed into gainful production. With the increasing use of machinery, however, these men and women are denied the opportunity of making a decent livelihood. I say, Mr. Speaker-and I am arguing for a shorter work day-that if as a result of the ingenuity of man during past generations we have reached the stage in our civilization when we can produce such a superabundance beyond our own requirements, then man ought to have the benefit of these scientific inventions, and that benefit should be in the form of giving the individual greater leisure than he has at the present time.
The forty-eight hour week, as provided for in this measure, does not give us very much. In a few isolated instances across this country those who to-day are working a little longer
Eight Hour Day-Mr. Heaps

than, forty-eight hours a week may be affected. There are not very many of them; my hon. friena from Bow River (Mr. Garland) suggests night watchmen and members of parliament. I think very few unemployed would be absorbed into industry in those few instances. If we are really to give useful work to our unemployed there must be a considerable reduction in the hours of labour, much below the forty-eight hours suggested in the present bill. I say this in spite of the fact that I give the measure my blessing and am happy, m a way, to see it introduced in parliament. I venture to assert, and this has been stated by many economists, that if we would absorb into productive employment these men and women who are to-day out of work and we put them all doing something useful, a three hour day might be sufficient to satisfy human requirements, but I am quite prepared on the present occasion to compromise on the six hour basis. In the United States at the present time there is before the Senate a bill for a six hour day being favourably considered. Why should we be behind the United States? There a similar bill was reported favourably upon last year, and the men who introduced that bill before the Senate and argued in its favour took the very same stand that I am taking here this afternoon, that if we are ever going to get back to anything approaching normal there has to be a shorter working week and a considerable increase in the purchasing power of the great masses of our people. I believe the very fact of this bill being introduced here this afternoon is a recognition of that principle, and the only difference I suppose now between the different groups in this house, if the house accepts the principle of a shorter working week, is the number of hours per week that should be worked in order to absorb the unemployed workers of this dominion.
So far as I am concerned and in this I am speaking I believe for those in this corner of the house, I am strongly opposed to the curtailment of production in whatever shape or form it may take, whether on the farm or in the factory or in the work shop. It is a form of industrial sabotage to which I am totally opposed, for I feel that the greater our productive capacity and the more we produce the better it ought to be for all concerned. But unfortunately that has not been the case during the past few years in this Dominion of Canada, nor for that matter in any other part of the world.
The hours of labour ought to be regulated according to the needs of the times. If through some catastrophe that might take

place the average workman in this country were called upon to work eight or ten or twelve hours a day, he would be glad to work to the utmost of his capacity provided there was the need for it, but on the other hand when there is no need for it, the great masses of our people should be given the advantage and blessing of modem invention, modern ingenuity and modern equipment.
Then there ought to be some close relationship between our productive capacity and our consumptive opportunities. To-day there is absolutely no relationship between the two. We produce goods in abundance in a haphazard way and then let them lie on our shelves and go to waste or sometimes rot while our people throughout the country are wanting these very goods but have no opportunity of consuming them. In my opinion a thirty hour week would be more than sufficient, so far as our work shops and our factories are concerned, to produce all that we could reasonably consume here in this dominion. I say that there must be a reasonable balance between production and consumption, with production always a little ahead of consumption.
I know that some people might say, and say with certain justification, that in the United States they have tried certain experiments which were not successful. Speaking in this house a little over a year ago, I said then that I did not expect very much success from the experiments that were being made in the United States because what they were doing there was trying to increase production ostensibly in order to absorb labour. The result was that the machine worked and profits were greater as a result of the increased production, and very little of the benefit of that increased production went to those who were actually engaged in a productive capacity.
Secondly, in the United States they tried to make codes and regulations, to establish a sort of cooperative system within the confines of the competitive, and sooner or lateT one had to give way to the other. Either the competitive had to give way to the cooperative, or the cooperative had to give way to the competitive. The result in the United States was that the cooperative efforts that were attempted to be established soon had to give way to the competitive, and the competitive system ran wild, with the consequent chaos that we see in the United States today.
Personally I would like to see us avoid the chaos that they have gone through in the United States, and I think it could be done if the government would give serious study

Eight Hour Day-Mr. Heaps
to some of the points I have outlined in my remarks here this afternoon. We are borrowing vast sums of money, just as they did in the United States. I have forgotten how many billions of dollars the United States has borrowed in the effort to borrow themselves back into prosperity. No nation can borrow itself back into prosperity. That is false economics all the way through, for the more they borrow the more they owe, the greater their indebtedness and the greater the load, and the moment the borrowing ceases you revert back to a condition which may well be worse than the first. There is an obvious reason for that. As long as you are living on borrowed money there is a fictitious sort of prosperity, but the moment the money that was borrowed has been spent and you have to pay it back, the conditions become entirely different. Therefore I say that we must get down to something more fundamental than the borrowing of money to bring about a prosperous condition among our people. As I have pointed out in this house year after year, there is to-day a huge gap between our production and our consumption. I said a few moments ago I am opposed to cutting down on production. What I want to see is an increase of the consumptive opportunities of our people throughout the length and breadth of this dominion, and by increasing those consumptive opportunities we shall be able to keep the industrial machine going, though I am free to admit, it may interfere with the large profits of those who own the machinery of production and distribution. But if in this house one has got to choose between the profits of a few individuals and the well-being of the great masses of our people, I am compelled to choose and be on the side of the masses of the people of this dominion.
It may be argued that a shorter work day will increase price levels and may perhaps hurt the position of the farmer, but I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that the farmer can be hurt very much more than he is at the present time. I as one coming from an industrial constituency, elected as a labour member and representing a labour constituency, am just as anxious for the farmer to be placed in a sound and secure position as I am to see the man in the industrial centres enjoy that security which he lacks at the present time. Price levels, important as they are, are not the all-important thing. I think the most important thing i.s to put into consumptive channels the goods we produce. In other words, there has to be a more equitable distribution of our wealth production in this dominion. The wealth of
a nation is not determined by price levels. The wealth of a nation is determined in the first place by the wealth that nation has within its geographical borders, its mines, its forests, its fields, its factories and its work shops. They are wealth, or potential wealth, and when the hand of man is put to these raw materials and potential wealth he produces the essential things of life. We are not short of wealth in this country, whether the price level is high or low. I was in 'Germany in 1923 when the price level was abnormally high, and just for an ordinary collar I would pay may be one quarter of a million marks, but that extraordinary high price level did not bring about prosperity in Germany. Nor does a low price level bring prosperity to the people of China. Prosperity can only come with high productive capacity, and when the results of that production are equally distributed among the people of that country, and that is exactly what I want to see in this dominion. We have that high productive capacity, and let us now bend our energies towards distributing our wealth production amongst the people who produce it so that they may enjoy the results of their labour.
We find that in this country we have more clothing probably than we know what to do with. We can produce clothing in abundance right from the raw materials almost through to the finished product. We have more wheat than the farmer knows what to do with. But the farmer cannot get the clothing he requires, and the man in the city has a mighty difficult task to get the flour to make into the bread that he needs. The only body that can deal with a question of this character is this parliament. We are the only logical body to deal with it, and any jurisdictional difficulties that might arise I think are infinitesimal as compared with the difficulty which the Canadian people have to-day in making a decent livelihood and finding a certain amount of security in life. To-day they have neither the opportunity of making a decent livelihood nor the opportunity of obtaining any security in life. Private initiative has failed completely in this respect just the same as it has failed in the United States during the past two years. Our people are compelled therefore to look to parliament as the only place where redress can be obtained. The provincial governments say that they cannot act in the matter and in spite of what some hon. members may say as to the difficulties presented by our constitution, I feel sure that if this parliament will show the

Eight Hour Day-Mr. Heaps
ways and means of grappling with the unemployment situation in a serious way none of the provincial authorities will question its jurisdiction.
Just as in the case of an eight hour day, a six hour day will mean more control and regulation and possibly more ownership of certain things by this parliament. After all there is not a very great gap between control and regulation and ownership. I do not contend that those who are in control or ownership of. industry are anxious to see unem-plojonent in our midst because I believe that if they had the power to eliminate it they would do so immediately. But the power of coping with this grave situation which now exists is beyond the control of the employers of labour.
Hon. members on the government side have referred to the new social order which will be created by this legislation but I cannot see that this legislation, the unemployment insurance legislation or other legislation which has been brought down ushers in a new social order. They .may prove a fine gesture but I am afraid they will not go far in overcoming the difficulties of the situation.
The amendment which I propose to move to the motion for third reading will reduce the hours of work per week from forty-eight to thirty. I submit that this parliament could do something which will offer redress to those men and women who find themselves out of work. I venture to assert that should the forty-eight hour legislation become effective within the next few months very few additional men and women will be absorbed into industry. After all, the important question to be considered is : How many more people will find work? Perhaps I had better read my amendment in order to give hon. members an opportunity of seeing what it contains. I intend to move, seconded by Mr. Maclnnis:
That all the words after "that" be struck out, and the following be substituted therefor:
"Bill No. 21 be referred' back to the committee of the whole with instructions that they have power to amend same by striking out the words 'forty-eight' where they appear in the said bill and substituting the word 'thirty' therefor, and also by striking out the word 'eight' where it appears and substituting the word 'six' therefor."
The adoption of this amendment would reduce the hours of work from forty-eight per week to thirty per week by means of a five day week of six hours each. I hope the government will give this matter sympathetic consideration. As I said a moment ago, in

the United States at the present time the government is considering the adoption of a six hour day. This matter was reported on favourably last year and I have every reason to believe that this year that government will pass legislation to enact a thirty hour week. Not only does the resolution now before the Senate of the United States provide for a thirty hour week but it stipulates that there shall be no reduction in pay. In other words, a person receiving S25 per week for a forty hour week would receive the same wages for a thirty hour week.

Mr. Speaker, it strikes me that the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) is moving an amendment which, if carried, would cause more unemployment. In fact, it would bring about the bankruptcy of all our industries. I am sympathetic with the objects which seem to be in the mind of the hon. member for North Winnipeg but under the industrial system which we have at the present time and in which the profit motive is the dominant one, how can we expect to have more employment if we ask the employer of labour to pay more for less? That is what this amendment means. If it asked that the whole matter of hours of employment be referred to the League of Nations, then I think any hon. member with any element of logic in his makeup could support the motion.
During the course of the remarks of the last speaker I was talking with a gentleman who has quite a lot to do with industry in this country. He told me that during the last four years he lost practically all the reserves which had been built up, a total of over a quarter of a million dollars. I wonder if those who are employed in the country at the present time really expect, except with the advent of socialism to-morrow, that any employer will pay them just as much money as they are paying them to-day for a shorter day of work or for less production. And after all, is not the prosperity of this nation based largely upon the possibility of the expansion of our export trade? I have heard my learned friend-

speechtext: I am not learned.

subtopic: BILL TO LIMIT HOURS OF WORK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
Well, he is very learned, in fact if not by courtesy, and I have heard him say that he was not in favour of tariffs but of world trade. Surely if you are in favour of world trade you are in favour of this country participating in world trade, and why should you put this country on the basis

Eight Hour Day-Mr. Stitt (Selkirk)
of more expensive production and expect it to obtain a larger share of the world's market? How is that possible in a world which is dominated by the profit motive? This resolution, if it were passed and if proper laws were enacted to enforce it in this country, would be the last step under our present system and the first step to complete socialism, and in my opinion it would lead to chaos. I think that is what it means. I want my hon. friend from North Winnipeg to realize this. I know that as time goes on, even at present, we ought to have fewer hours of labour; there is no doubt about that. But how can we get so far ahead of world progress so long as we have to bear in mind the existence of the profit motive? Why do men go into business? Why does any man work? Under our system men work for wages, and they establish industries and go into trade for the purpose of making profits. Employment is all based on the wage motive or the profit motive. I believe that if the resolution were passed and if this country set up the necessary administrative machinery to enforce it there would be more unemployment to-morrow than there is to-day and there would be chaos.

speechtext: Can the hon. member tell me why they are trying to do it in the United States?

subtopic: BILL TO LIMIT HOURS OF WORK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: Are they trying?

subtopic: BILL TO LIMIT HOURS OF WORK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: Certainly. It is now before the Senate.

speechtext:
The United States is practically in the position where its whole export trade only amounts to between eight and ten per cent of its entire business. Look at the wheat situation in this country, however. The United States is a far more self-contained nation than we are. Suppose we applied the six hour day to agriculture, considering the difficulty we have at the present time in getting any kind of reasonable price for our wheat. Suppose we increased the farmer's cost. This resolution if enacted would increase the cost of every commodity that enters into every kind of production including agriculture. The farmer's machinery would cost more; transportation would cost more; everything he uses would cost more. remedy the situation, why should we forget the facts and in a measure of abstract idealism bring ruin to the whole industrial and trading fabric of the nation? How can you ask an industry which is exporting agricultural implements or automobiles to compete with Japan at the present time and reduce its hours of labour by thirty-three per cent and increase its cost? And I believe that is what would happen if this proposal were enacted. What about human nature? What about the railway men at the present time? The railway men who are employed want to run their 3,600 miles a month. They do not want to cut down their right to earn money and to have the work distributed to their brothers who are out of employment. Although ideally they preach that doctrine they do not live up to it in practice.
I think the object which the hon. member has in view is perfectly laudable and there should be a reduction in the hours of labour. First I may say that with some of the views expressed by my hon. friend I would be in agreement. It is true that the labour people in the world today are not much interested in a forty-eight hour week as was indicated last year at the international labour conference where a draft convention was submitted for a forty hour work week and, as I said on the second reading of this bill or when the draft convention was submitted to the house, was adopted by the convention but failed of having any effect because there was not the quorum required by the rules of the conference owing to the fact that most of the government delegates, including the one representing Canada, were absent when the vote was taken. However the conference adopted a resolution to place this draft convention upon the agenda for the next conference which takes place in a week or two. This will be the first matter to be considered there, and the government might have waited until this draft convention is disposed of by the labour conference before dealing with this matter. However we have before the house this bill for a forty-eight hour week, and the government is basing this legislation on the draft convention adopted at Washington in 1919. This is part of the preamble of the bill:
Whereas a draft convention respecting hours of work in industrial undertakings was agreed upon at a general conference of the international labour organization of the league of nations, in accordance with the relevant articles of the said treaty, -which said convention has been ratified by Canada; and whereas^ it is advisable to enact the necessary legislation to enable Canada to discharge the obligations assumed under the provisions of the said treaty-

[Mr. J. H. Stitt. 1

speechtext:
On every occasion I
believe when organized labour appeared before the various governments of this country since the approval of the draft convention at Washington, organized labour has urged the passage of a measure such as is before the house to-day; organized labour has asked for a forty-eight hour week and an eight hour day. When that draft convention was approved at Washington, there was a very large gathering of representatives of the various countries of the world that had become signatories to the treaty. The

Eight Hour Day-Mr. Gordon
Labour Gazette of December, 1919, in reporting that labour conference at Washington has this to say at page 1425:
The first international labour conference, convened under the authority of the treaty of peace, assembled in Washington, D.C., on October 29, and concluded its labours exactly one month later on November 29, The purpose of this organization is to promote the international regulation of labour conditions.
It was the first time that representatives of governments, and of employing and employed interests assembled in an international conference to consider labour problems. The agenda of this first conference had been fixed in the peace treaty and the proceedings in Washington were entirely confined thereto. The matters under consideration related to the permanent organization of the international labour body and the following specific subjects of reference, namely: The application in the countries represented of the principle of the eight hour day or forty-eight hour week, the question of preventing or providing against unemployment, various proposals relating to the employment of women and children. Considering the diversity of the interests represented, it was the general feeling that the discussions and decisions of the conference gave evidence of a sincere desire on the part of the participants to fulfil the purposes for which the organization had been created.
I would like to draw the attention of hon. members to the last paragraph:
The conference gave evidence of a sincere desire on the part of the participants to fulfil the purposes for which the organization had been created.
Then the report goes on:
The following general principles are enunciated in the treaty of peace as comprising the methods and principles for regulating industrial conditions which all industrial communities should endeavour to apply so far as their special circumstances will permit.
It proceeds then with quotations from the treaty itself.
The high contracting parties,-
And Canada was one of them:
-recognizing that the well being, physical, moral and intelleeutal, of industrial wage earners is of supreme international importance have framed, in order to further this great end, the permanent machinery provided for in section I and asociated with that of the League of Nations.
With that general thought in view the conference proceeded with its labours. We had at that conference a very large and very representative body of delegates and advisers, numbering twenty-six in all. They included Hon. G. D. Robertson, Minister of Labour for Canada, and Hon. Newton W. Rowell as government delegates. We had as advisers, F. A Acland, Deputy Minister of Labour, 92582-130J
Mr. Loring G. Christie, Mr. Daniel A. Cameron, Hon. C. W. Robinson, Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, Mr. Louis Guyon, Doctor Walter A. Riddell, Hon. Thomas H. Johnson, Mr. T. M. Molloy, Hon. C. R. Mitchell, Mr. J. D. McNiven, Mr. Gerald H. Brown, Mr. S.	R. Parsons, Mr. Sam Harris, Mr. J. T. Stirrett, Mr. E. Blake Robertson, Mr. J. B. Hugg, Mr. J. G. Merrick, Mr. P. M. Draper, Mr. Tom Moore, Mr. Arthur Martel, Mr. Robert Baxter, Mr. David Rees, Mrs. Kathleen Derry. So hon. members will see that Canada was represented at that conference by very eminent persons, meeting for the purpose of formulating and adopting draft conventions, and unquestionably assuming some responsibility to see that those draft conventions were something more than mere expressions of pious wishes. Certainly there must have been some assumption of obligation on everyone represented there to see that these draft conventions were ultimately given effect to in the countries to which they applied. Now the right hon. leader of the opposition was at that conference, and doubtless displayed his usual activity. I think I can surmise that he took a very active part in seeing that that draft convention was brought into being and carefully revised.
As I say, year after year organized labour m Canada has asked that that draft convention be given effect to. What was the result? Less than three years afterwards the government in Canada changed and a Liberal government came into power. What was the attitude of that government with respect to these draft conventions which have become the subject matter of legislation during this session of parliament? They went into the depths of cold storage. Nothing was ever done to bring them into effect. Yet the right hon. leader of the opposition, always interested, like the rest of us I hope, in promoting peace and good will in the world, and professing a desire, and I believe trying at times to do something for labour-I do not want to detract from what the right hon. leader of the opposition has done-with respect to these draft conventions he did nothing. During those intervening years from 1922 until a few weeks ago, the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) was one of the foremost men in Canada advocating the League of Nations, the treaty of peace and all these complementary things that have to do with them. Now what happens? The very moment a government in Canada seeks to give effect to these draft conventions the right hon. leader of the opposition drags out

old ultra vires, and the hon. member for Quebec East resigns from leadership of the League of Nations society in Canada.

Now, as to this amendment if the government is right in its legal position that, having become a signatory to the peace treaty and having approved and adopted a draft convention in this parliament and having by reason thereof a right to found legislation upon the convention, then of necessity if the government's view is to prevail it must follow the terms of that convention in substance. But the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) advances an amendment which by its very terms will place those who seek to impeach this bill in the position that suits their purpose, that of being able to say that we have departed completely from the convention. The amendment would enable them to advance that argument before the courts as a reason why this legislation should be declared ultra vires of the dominion parliament. I do not know why my hon. friend advanced that amendment, for he must have known what its effect would be.
For my part I suggest that working hours should be reduced just as rapidly as can be done with safety, but that it would not be of benefit to the working people of this country to assume deliberately an attitude that will nullify this great forward step, as I believe it is, of placing in the power of this parliament through our participation in the League of Nations the right to control these very vital matters that experience is disclosing must in a measure be controlled by the central authority. I am not going to endeavour to go into the legal position concerning this bill. I have heard it discussed here, I have read the discussions in another place in parliament. I think I have said before that we can learn a lot of law from all the discussions. But when I find very eminent legal gentlemen such as the hon. member for Quebec East, very eminent constitutional authorities such as the right hon. leader of the opposition, and very eminent lawyers like the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and the leader of the Senate, not seeing exactly eye to eye on this question, I get some comfort out of the thought that, while I am sure this legislation is within our competence, I feel so

for reasons different from those expressed by these other gentlemen. So we have a pretty general disagreement of opinion both here and in the Senate.
I think this legislation will stand the test of our courts. The hon. member for Quebec East says a further measure is now pending before this same tribunal which will still further reduce the hours of labour, and he suggests that we should wait until we see the fate of that further convention before proceeding with this measure. I think the sound course, if the government is right, is to go ahead now, adopt this convention and, have it understood across Canada that, through the agency of this treaty, the federal parliament has the right to do what we are now doing. Then if at some near future date the international labour organization, with all the nations of the world represented, comes to the conclusion that a further or different arrangement can be safely offered to the signatories of the treaty and those nations that are members of the labour organization, then it will be time for this parliament to undertake to draft legislation founded on that new convention.

Possibly my hon. friend may be correct; I would be representing Prince Edward Island in this house at the time, but I am quite distinct in my mind that it was due at least in part to the fact that both Hon. N. W. Rowell and Senator Robertson knew I had been Minister of Labour and deputy minister for a number of years, and was interested in these matters, that the invitation came to be extended to me to be one of the advisers at the conference at Washington. My hon. friend the Minister of Labour read to the house the list of those present. As he was reading it my colleague the ex-Minister of Justice remarked that there was a very large number of representatives from Canada. I gave my colleague the answer as to why the list- was so large, and I will give it to this house. It was assumed at that time, as all of us, on this side at least, assumed up to the beginning of this year, that matters respecting hours of labour came within the jurisdiction of the different provinces, and for that reason all the provinces of Canada were asked to be represented at the international conference in Washington. That, by the way, will explain how my attendance as an adviser came to, be in connection with the province of Prince Edward Island; I was one of the provincial representatives duly authorized by the provincial government. I am quite sure that as representing Prince Edward Island at the time I would have taken and did take the position that the enactment of legislation respecting the eight hour day came within the jurisdiction of the government of that province.
At any rate I know that all those who were present, both the ministers of the crown representing the federal government at the time and the representatives of the several provinces, were of one mind with respect to which legislative body had the competent jurisdiction in the matter of dealing with hours of labour. While all were equally desirous of seeing an eight hour day generally applied in Canada, I know all were equally of the view that if it were to be part of the law of this land, it would have to be enacted via the provincial legislatures in the first
instance. The procedure laid down by the international labour organization, as fashioned by the League of Nations, was that the draft conventions, in the first instance, would in federal states come to the federal government and later where necessary because of jurisdiction would be referred by the federal government to the different provinces.
Now may I point out that this meeting in Washington was held in 1919. It was December, 1921, before the Liberal administration took office; until that time either the Union government of Sir Robert Borden or the Conservative government of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen was in office. If hon. members will look at the records of the privy council for that period they will find that the then Minister of Justice, Hon. Mr. Doherty, was responsible for the order in council which set forth the method the government of Canada should adopt with respect to the various conventions that came from the labour conference. I placed that order in council on record when I was speaking previously, so I need not read it now; it will be found in the remarks I made at the time the first draft convention was discussed during this present session of parliament. It distinctly set out-and this by a Conservative minister of justice-that the obligation of the federal parliament with respect to these conventions concerning hours of labour and the like was to transfer them to the competent legislative authority of this country, and that the competent legislative authority with respect to the eight hour day was the provincial governments. Hon. gentlemen will find that Hon. Mr. Doherty and the Conservative government of the day fulfilled the obligation, as they then understood it, by seeing that the draft convention respecting the eight hour day was referred to the various provinces. If other governments that have succeeded have taken a similar course it is because each and every one has been advised by the law officers of the crown that that was the proper method to pursue.
The Minister of Labour says these draft conventions were kept in cold storage from 1921 to 1930, and I can only speak for that period. From our point of view they were not kept in cold storage at all; they were referred, as the law officers advised the treaty obligations required, to the various provinces. During that period of time the Liberal government had many conferences with the provinces, some of which specifically considered the question of whether among themselves the provinces coulld not agree to see that, as between themselves there would be uniformity

So that far from having draft conventions in cold storage we were doing our utmost during our time t'o see that they were enacted, that they were not allowed to remain mere recommendations, but that in so far as it was possible for the federal government to influence the provinces, the provinces would be influenced in the direction of carrying them out. As a matter of fact, most of the provinces had already enacted all that was requested. But since my hon. friend has spoken of cold storage, may I remind him that he and most of his colleagues have been members of the present government now for nearly five years, so according to his statement they have evidently been viewing these draft conventions as being left in cold storage. May I say this? When I made the statement the other day that we wished to see these measures enacted, I meant exactly what I said. I did not mean that we wished to

see a lot of make-believe legislation placed on the statute books. Similarly it could be made generally applicable by the British North America Act being amended so as to give this parliament power to pass legislation of this kind, amended with the consent of the provinces, which I believe could be and would be obtained, and would have been obtained long before this had hon. gentlemen opposite not needed that thawdng out process to which the Minister of Labour has just referred.

I think it is perfectly clear just why, of necessity, the position that I personally at any rate have taken in this matter has been what it is. It has been what it has among other reasons for the one cited by the Minister of Labour this afternoon, that I was present at the international conference that met at Washington when this matter was discussed and the draft convention framed, and I know that it was the view of dominion and provincial representatives alike that the eight hour day legislation so far as Canada was concerned, if it was to be enacted and made effective, would have to be provincial legislation.

Eight Hour Day-Mr. Hanson
The government is now hanging its whole case in regard to the possibility of this legislation being intra vires on the slender thread that this house has approved the draft convention. It is not any longer on the ground of the draft convention itself. The Minister of Justice this afternoon told us that the situation had altered since this house had approved the convention. That is the slender thread on which all of this social legislation hangs. I do not wish to use a term that will belittle what is being attempted here, but I do , say that in the absence of an authoritative basis, all that we are doing at the present time is putting ourselves in the position of passing so much make-believe legislation.
I am anxious, nevertheless, to have this legislation, such as it is, given the best possible chance that it can have before the courts, and for that reason I would not wish to, prejudice its chances, however slight, by supporting the amendment which has been moved this afternoon by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps). That amendment, as has been stated by the Minister of Labour this afternoon, is altogether beyond the scope or provisions of the draft convention, and consequently beyond the grounds on which the government says it has any authority whatever to deal with this matter. Assuming that my hon. friend's amendment were to pass and the bill were to be modified as he suggests and that later on it were to come before the courts, where the argument would be made which the government has urged this afternoon, that because this parliament has approved of the convention we have the power to legislate, and with nothing more than that to support it; what would become of the whole legislation? Mr. Speaker, from the remarks which have been made on both sides of the house it is quite evident that both major parties intend to vote against the amendment moved by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps). Therefore, I suppose that anyone who now stands up and says that he is going to vote for the amendment will be liable to the charge that he is playing the cheaper kind of politics in making an appeal to his labour constituents when he has full knowledge that this amendment will not pass. I shall have to take that risk because I intend to vote for the amendment. Briefly, I shall state my reasons for voting in this way.
The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stitt) argued that the passage of this amendment would mean more unemployment rather than

Eight Hour Day-Mr. Neill
the creating of more employment. He went on to say that those who worked only six hours would not be able to compete with those who worked eight hours. This argument must be at least one hundred years old and there are hundreds of pages of history dealing with it. At one time little children and women in the nail making industry in Lancashire were forced to work stripped to their waists because of the intense heat. They had to work twelve and fourteen hours a day and it was suggested that these women and children of eight to ten years of age should not have to work such long hours under such conditions. Hundreds of pages of the press of that day were filled with the same argument which we recognize as being offered this afternoon in a more moderate form. This afternoon, the question was asked: What would happen to the industries? It was stated that they would all be ruined.
There is much truth in the statement that in order to be truly successful such legislation should be universal or nearly universal. This may be so but are we to wait forever until the other man or the other nation gives the lead? The hon. member for North Winnipeg stated that legislation was pending in the Senate of the United States which looks toward a six hour day. The former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) stated that a similar suggestion was being placed on the agenda of the next meeting of the League of Nations. What would be the effect in Washington and Geneva if this house passed the resolution proposed by the hon. member for North Winnipeg? Would it not give them a tremendous lead to go and do likewise? I care not who opposes the idea, or however able he may be, it is obvious that labour will never be able to take up the slack caused by the efficiency of machinery unless by means of shorter hours. No matter what other palliative you suggest, that is the crucial and final remedy-shorter and shorter hours for everybody.
It is said that the matter is one of provincial jurisdiction. Well, it is much harder to start anything like this under provincial jurisdiction than it is in the larger unit of the dominion, because the larger the unit the more likely will the step be successful. If it were done by a province they could not compete in the production of goods or of raw products with a neighbouring province or state in which there were longer hours. So that the larger the unit under which it is first begun, the more likely it is to be successful.
The Minister of Labour, the ex-Minister of Justice and the leader of the opposition said that the passage of this amendment would imperil the whole act, and from the arguments adduced I think that is probably correct. The passage of this amendment might result in the whole act being disavowed. But I do not think that is so very important, because the eight hour day is general throughout the country now. But if this amendment were adopted it would be important as a gesture; it would be significant if this house adopted the proposal and took a definite stand in favour of shorter hours. We are liable to be brought into the position recorded in one of the books of the Apocalypse or somewhere else-I forget precisely where. There was a great revival on the earth, threatening to assume considerable proportions and to be highly successful, and Satan gathered his satellites around him and said that something must be done about it. He said he would give a prize to anyone who would suggest a scheme which he might carry to the earth and put into practice. One devil said, "Send me;
I will tell them there is no God." Satan replied, "You are a fool, for everyone knows that there is a God." Another devil said. "Send me; I will tell them there is no hell" and Satan replied, "You also are wrong, because everyone knows there is a hell and there are a good many people living in it now." Finally one wizened, old devil in the background said, "Send me; I will tell them there is a God and there is a hell and a heaven, but I will tell them there is lots of time." Satan replied that he was the man, and he was sent and the revival was defeated. That is the sort of danger we are going to be in. We are all in favour of shorter hours as an ideal; that is the standard we are aiming at; but we are going to stand by and say there's lots of time yet, and that will kill the effort, without any question. I do not for a moment suggest that the Minister of Labour is not sincere when he says that it is his ambition to see the proposal adopted. But the danger is that if we do not deal with it drastically and firmly it will never be done. I firmly believe that even supposing this bill were declared ultra vires parliament would be doing a splendid thing and setting an example to the rest of the world, if the proposal were adopted. It would be a step towards the rehabilitation of civilization, even if it resulted in the act being declared ultra vires, because as I say, it would be a gesture and would give a lead to the other nations of the world. The very news that Canada, the largest dominion in the British empire, had

Mr. Chairman, a few years ago the Canada Grain Act was amended so as to prohibit the mixing of wheat in grades Nos. 1, 2 and 3 northern, and before this vote is carried I hope the minister will tell us what steps are being taken by the grain commission to see that that provision of the Canada Grain Act is being carried out.
While I am on my feet there is another matter I should like to bring to the attention of the committee. Even if those provisions for the prevention of mixing may be carried out, another practice apparently has grown up which lowers the standard of No. 1 and No. 2 northern in particular so far as shipments overseas are concerned. It is quite a common practice, I am told, for cars <5f No. 1 and No. 2 northern wheat which are sampled at Winnipeg to be tested for protein content by the grain companies. Word is sent ahead to the terminal at Fort William, and if this wheat is of a high protein content in many cases it is binned by itself and certain bins apparently are held for what is called selected No. 1 northern, high protein. The result of this practice, it seems to me, must be to lower the grade of the bulk of the wheat that goes out to our overseas customers. I assume that most of this selected wheat is shipped to the United States. I do not know whether the commission are aware of what is going on, but I take it for granted that they are. I Should like to know whether they approve of this practice, whether they have any way of stopping it, and whether they think it should be allowed to continue. I have in my hand some of the loading orders that are issued by one of the grain companies at Fort William. They are really instructions to their elevator man to load so many thousand bushels of selected No. 1 northern into a certain hold of a steamer, and I have seen enough of these orders to convince me that this is quite a common practice.
There is another matter with which I might as well deal while I am on my feet, and it is in connection with the grading of durum wheat. I do not think the law prevents the mixing of the various grades of durum wheat, and possibly there is a great deal of mixing being done. The factor that determines the grade of durum wheat is mainly the amount of spring wheat it may contain. The definition of No. 1 durum is set forth in the act. It may contain a maximum of five per cent of spring wheat, and that is increased up to an additional [Mr. Mackenzie King.J
five per cent for the lower grades. But whatever grades of durum are received in the private terminals, I do not think there is very much -durum wheat shipped out except that which goes out as No. 1. So it does appear that there is more No. 1 durum going out than there is going in. The average quality of the No. 1 durum which is being shipped out cannot in that case be as high as it would be if the mixing were not permitted, and the elevator companies had to ship out the same quantity of each grade that they took in. It does seem as though there was a great deal of mixing of -durum wheats, and it is almost self evident, I think, that it would be to the advantage of the grower of the high grade durum wheat if the elvators were not allowed to mix the lower grades with it and then put it all out as high grade wheat. I am told that in some of the terminal elevators they have machines for taking out the ragweed, I think it is. They use water to float this weed seed out of the wheat, and the result is that the wheat w-hic-h has been through the water carries a pretty heavy percentage of moisture, but they are able to mix it with the No. 1 straight durum and still have a moisture content of the whole mixture that is not higher than that allowed under the act.
These are two questions particularly that I wish the minister to deal with. Are these practices being carried on; if so does the commission see any objection to them, and have they any -way of dealing with the matter to see that the average grade of the wheat going out of the terminal, in the case of both northern wheat and durum wheat, is as good as that of the wheat that -goes in under the different grades? Further, do the commission approve of the practice of special binning for high protein wheat and the mixing of the durum wheat which I belie-ve is going on in the private terminals at Fort William?
Hon. R. B. HAiN-SON (Minister of Trade and 'Commerce):	The hon. gentleman has
put on the record a considerable number of questions, and I shall deal with them in the order in which he has raised them.
First with respe-ct to the amendments which were made to the grain act last year in relation to garnet wheat, it is the intention o-f the government so far as I am aware to allow the legislation to go into effect, but the matter has not been finally concluded and consideration is being given to representations which have been made -from time to time during the last few weeks as the time approaches when the amendments to the a-ct are to go into effect.

Supply-Trade-Grain Act
With respect to the second matter to which my hon. friend alluded, namely, the special binning of wheat at terminal elevators, I am advised that a perusal of the grain act will show that this is a perfectly legal process under the provisions of the act itself. This special binning of select wheats by terminal elevators is legal under the grain act and is controlled by the commissioners, in so far as the special bins leased for this purpose have to be authorized by them. It would not appear that this matter is of any considerable importance, because out of a total of 62,000,000 bushels which came to the head of the lakes during the past season, only
820,000	bushels have been so binned. This is only about one and one quarter per cent of the total. This facility of special binning is open to all interests, including the Canadian mills. In order to specially bin wheat it is necessary for the purchaser to obtain the owner's consent, thereby assuring an equitable return of the premium paid in this connection. An objectionable practice which was stopped in 1930 was that of permitting the diverting of special wheat without the owner's consent and frequently without any premium compensation being paid to the owner. I am advised by the commission that the only possible objection to this practice is that it more or less reduces the average quality of the outgoing shipments, that is the shipments which go to the export trade. However, this has not assumed such proportions as to make it important. Furthermore, the principle of the owner of the wheat disposing of it to the best advantage has not yet been set aside by the grain act.
With respect to the third matter to which the hon. member referred, I understand that the mixing of durum wheat is legalized by the statute. The commission had applied to the grain standards committee for the setting up of an out-turn standard, but this was rejected.

I should like to know what steps are being taken or have been taken by the grain commission to see that no mixing occurs in the terminal of numbers 1, 2 and 3 northern?
Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury) I am advised that they weigh out the elevators annually and check that with the warehouse receipts. This would appear to be all that they can do. I am further advised that the practice of mixing durum is not very general although it is permitted to a degree.

This matter was discussed in the committee, where it was contended that if mixing was prohibited the services of an army of inspectors would be required to see that the provision was carried out. I have been asked on more than one occasion to inquire if the commission really knew whether mixing was going on.

I am advised by the chairman that he is personally satisfied that there is no mixing of the grades to which the hon. member alluded. Unless the hon. member has evidence to that effect I think he should accept the chairman's statement.

I have no evidence that it is being done, but I should like to know if the commission could tell us at any time the number of bushels of each grade which may be shipped into the terminals at the head of the lakes and the number of bushels which may be shipped out?
I do not know that that information is available at the moment, but it will be produced by the chairman.

Some time ago I had a question on the order paper asking for the number of bushels of each grade of durum wheat which was graded into the terminals and the number of bushels graded out. As I remember the answer, it was to the effect that the commission did not have that information.
I do not recall the question, but I am advised by the chairman of the commission that that information can be obtained and I will see that the hon. member gets it.
Can that be given for the private terminals?
No, only the public and semi-public.
I understand that the government elevator at Port Arthur has been leased. Is it being run as a private or as a public terminal?
As a semipublic terminal.
The figures would be available as to the in-turn and out-turn of that elevator?	[DOT]
Yes.

Can the minister give us the terms upon which that elevator was leased?

I think the answer to that question was put on the record a short time ago.

I understand that numbers 1, 2 and 3 northern are checked into these terminal elevators and then they are weighed out at the end of the season, and if the weigh-out does not come up to a certain percentage, or if it does not balance within a certain percentage, the amount which happens to be over is confiscated or taken away. Could the minister advise the committee the leeway allowed and the amounts which have been confiscated in different years?

give me the number of bushels of w'heat which will be affected by giving a special grade to garnet wheat?
