are approximately 50,000,000 bushels of garnet wheat in the country at the present time, but I do not know how many bushels there will be on July 31.
[Mr Coote.]

I should like to ask the minister a question in connection with the strike of farmers in the Myrnam district in Alberta about a year ago. As the minister no doubt knows, this district is in the northern part of the province where there is a fairly good fall of rain. It occurs quite often that the grain comes out tough and the people in that vicinity were of the opinion that they were not getting a fair deal from the elevator companies. Practically all the farmers in that district went on strike and refused to deliver their grain. The board of grain commissioners were informed of this trouble and I believe went up to the district in an effort to settle the difficulty. I should like to know the findings of the committee and what was done in an effort to settle 'the difficulties which the farmers were facing at that time.
I do not think the hon. member is referring to Myrnam; I think he means the strike at Mundare, because the other was the year before.
I am referring to the one at Myrnam; the other is in the district represented by my hon. friend from Vegreville.

I have no information regarding the strike at Myrnam, but I have regarding the strike at Mundare in October, 1934, and that I will place at the disposal of the committee. With reference to the strike that occurred the previous year, I will get the information.

Each year that this item has been under discussion up to the present time I have inquired of the previous minister whether there was any evidence of the restored mixing of wheat grades. The practice was general years ago. The answer which that minister gave was invariably, no. Well, each year I hear further reports of it. I am not making any charge just now but I want to put the government on their guard. It is easy to start these practices but difficult to stop them. These practices invariably begin under Conservative governments and then it takes the succeeding government nearly all their time in office to stop them. In 1930 an attempt was made by some of us to prohibit the mixing of grades and a compromise was reached, prohibiting mixing in the four top northern grades and permitting it in the rest of the grades. As a matter of practice anything that is not prohibited under the grain act is usually done; that is the substance of the matter. It is not particularly made illegal, but it is not prohibited ana

Supply

Trade-Grain Act
therefore it is gone ahead with. I have grave suspicions and pretty reliable information that the law is being broken with respect to the four top grades. I did not hear the first remarks of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote), but I understood him to be drawing attention to the special binned top grades. These grades are isolated and special binned for their quality and are sent to the United States, where a premium is paid therefor. That is exactly the way it started before, only it was with carloads; carloads were switched and cut out and sent somewhere-usually to our millers. To the extent that that was done, what ivas exported overseas was correspondingly impoverished in quality.

I read to the committee a statement from the grain commission with respect to this question of special binning. I will not repeat the statement because the hon. member will read it in Hansard. I understand that this is quite legal under the act of 1930 which I believe the hon. gentleman himself piloted through the house.
I did not pilot it.
I take that back; it was the former Minister of Trade and Commerce.

I do not know that special binning is absolutely prohibited, and anything that is not prohibited the elevators always do if it suits them. But special binning, I understand, is being done on the protein basis. High protein cars are specially binned, and a guarantee of a certain protein content is sold to the millers in the United States, who pay a premium thereon. When the wheat is bought from the farmer he does not know what the protein content is and it is nonsense to say that the premium goes to the producer; it goes to the mixer or special binner. Furthermore, it impoverishes the great bulk of the wheat that goes overseas, where we have the keenest competition. It certainly violates the spirit of the act when you isolate the best type grades with the highest protein-and the value of our wheat is set by its protein content and quality of protein. That is what they are buying-protein-and when you isolate a lot of that and send it to one market, giving that market our choice wheat as to protein, you impoverish the great bulk of the wheat that goes overseas when the price is set. The more that is done the more you impoverish the rest of the wheat, and that is a violation of the spirit of the act. I understand it is being done right along.

No grain is special binned without the consent of the owner, and that ensures the premium to him if there is one. As regards the quantity of wheat special binned during the past season, it has been only about one and one-quarter per cent of the total output, so that it is not very large. As regards my hon. friend's point, that there is no guarantee that the premium goes to the producer, my information is that there shall be no special binning under the act without the consent of the owner, whoever he may be, whether producer or anyone else. He gets the premium, and that is the intention.
No; the minister is entirely wrong. The grower does not get it.
I said owner.

I contend that the grower does not get it. Once it passes out of his hands the owner gets the premium because of the privilege of special binning. Under the act it is regrettable that we do not grade our wheat according to protein content, and until that is done you cannot pass the premium on to the grower. The present abuse cannot be prevented under the act as it stands; it is quite legitimate. My point is that you cannot pass the premium on to the grower. I have no doubt that the percentage which the minister has mentioned-one and a quarter per cent-is correct, but still it deteriorates the great bulk of the wheat to that extent. If you take one and a quarter per cent of high protein content out of the wheat the rest of it deteriorates to that extent. I appreciate the point the minister is trying to make, but I contend that you cannot get the benefit to the grower; it goes to the man who buys it from the grower. The elevator may special bin it at the terminus, and that cannot be prevented under the act.

There is a good deal in what the hon. gentleman says: it all depends on who the owner is. In some instances the commission man probably does not pass it on, but I do not think that is the grain commission's concern. They cannot be charged with the distribution of the premium, but there is a premium and it goes to the owner, whoever he may be. As regards the degradation, by reason of this special binning, of the quantity that goes into the export trade, I agree with the hon. gentleman. But it is permitted by the act and I do not think that any great harm is done where the quantity is
Supply-Trade-Grain Act

so small. I believe that is the opinion of the commission. Of course, if it assumed larger proportions it would be a different matter.

Two years ago the different wheat exporting nations-Canada, the United States, the Argentine, and Australia- met at Rome and the secretary of our high commissioner in London attended as Canadian representative. At that meeting it was decided that all exporting nations should have a quota. Well, they did not decide at that time at Rome as to what the quota would be, and they adjourned to London. While they were there, they decided what the quota for the different nations would be. Our representative I understand was a lawyer from Regina. The quotas were set, but everybody came home and they practically decided to break the agreement; at least no one of whom I have knowledge has kept it. We did not sell our quota, but the Argentine republic sold theirs and more than theirs. Then we lent them some of ours, but the Prime Minister told us that we were to get this all back the next year. However the next year we did not get it back and the Argentine republic oversold their quota. We are now told that this commission business and the quota have all gone by the board and that all the money we have put up in this connection has been of no account whatever. I assume the minister will be able to give us a detailed statement in regard to all these matters; how this has happened; why we were told that this quota was to foe such a wonderful thing; why it is now all being abandoned and what we are going to do with our quota. I remember seeing somewhere in Hansard this statement made by the Prime Minister:
In any event it would be merely a loan of a part of our quota until next year, so that we would not lose anything if we made an adjustment with the Argentine.
In other words, we made a loan to the Argentine and were to get it back the following year. When are we going to get this loan back?
Any discussion on this particular question has no reference to the item before us. Furthermore, the quota system broke down because Argentina would not play the game with the other nations.

I think it would be very
unkind to compel the minister to give an explanation.

Perhaps
I am not as good at explaining as are some

other people, but I shall at least do my best. The quota system fell down because another nation did not keep the arrangement.
We did not ourselves.

That
may be true, but so far as this department and this appropriation are concerned, we have no responsibility in the matter.

That is not what the
hon. member for Willow Bunch has said-

I know
what he said.	[DOT]

The minister did not
understand it. The hon. member for Willow Bunch repeated what has been stated in the house by the Prime Minister, namely, that the quota was a certain quantity of wheat which Canada was allowed to sell and that she loaned part of her quota to Argentina. The question the hon. member for Willow Bunch has just put to the minister is this: First, what is the amount of wheat which was allowed for Canada's quota? Second, what amount was loaned to Argentina? Third, was it given back to Canada? I understood the hon. member very well; I was sitting next to him and I would like the minister to give a clear answer to that. I am ready to act as an interpreter at any time.

The hon.
member for Willow Bunch made his question quite clear and I answered it.
As regards this question of mixing, the hon. member for Melville said that he had a very strong suspicion that the law was being broken in connection with the four top grades. My information from the grain commission is that there is no mixing in the four top grades, and unless my hon. friend has evidence, the question should not be pursued further. If he has evidence, he ought in justice to all concerned to submit it and I will ask him to be good enough to do so.
I want to know plainly the position in which we stand at present in regard to the quota. Is this all gone by the board?

I shall
have to get the information for the hon. gentleman; I do not have it now.

I notice there is an
increase of about $170,000 in this estimate. How much did this conference at Rome cost us? How much money did we pay into this?

Supply-Trade-Grain Act
It is not dealt with in this appropriation at all.

What appropriation
does it come under?

I shall
have to find out; it does not come under my department.

It is the marketing of
wheat.

The
marketing of wheat does not come under the grain act, and nobody knows that better than does the hon. member for Willow Bunch.

Does the minister
mean to tell me that the Department of Trade and Commerce has nothing to do with the marketing of wheat?

We have
nothing to do with that.

What department does
it come under?
I shall have to find out. We do not sell wheat. So far as I know, no department of the government has anything to do with the marketing Of wheat.

We understand that perfectly, but- on the other hand the regulations concerning the marketing of wheat come under the Department of Trade and Commerce' and no other department that 1 know of. This is something new to us that is taking place.

The Department of Trade and Commerce has to do with the grading and warehousing of wheat. Any marketing of wheat that is going on in this country is under the auspices of the selling agency and that is all I have to say in regard to that.

That selling agency has existed only since it was put into operation by the present government. We have had private individuals marketing wheat for years and years, and there is no doubt that has all come under the Department of Trade and Commerce. We have always said that the marketing of grain should be under the Department of Agriculture instead of the Department of Trade and Commerce.
It comes under the Post Office Department; it is sold by parcel post.

The wheat selling agency was set up not by this government but by the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, commonly known as the wheat pool, and all this government has to do with the matter is in connection with the guarantees given to the banks under the relief act.
The pool agencies in the west do not cover more than half the quantity of wheat in western Canada. What happens to the rest? Do they dump it into the ocean or what do they do with it?
It goes out through the export agencies.
What department does that come under?
It does not come under any department; it is free from government control.

I just want to call attention to what the minister has said. He has said that the marketing of wheat does not come under his department or any other department of government. Perhaps hon. members will remember the charge that was made against the Minister of Trade and Commerce in the late government and the taunt that was hurled at him very frequently when he said that the government was not marketing wheat; that the wheat was marketing itself.
No; the hon. gentleman said that he was not interested in the marketing of wheat. That is slightly different.
The word "interested" was not used by the then minister.
My hon. friend was not in the house at that time and I was.

Nevertheless the taunt has been hurled against the then Minister of Trade and Commerce, that he said he had nothing to do with the marketing of wheat. That was the situation at that time. Now we talk about the marketing of wheat being under the sales agency, but there was no sales agency then. The other night when the hon. member for Lethbridge was discussing this matter he was entirely out of order or I would have taken the question up myself at the time,, when he stated that this government had marketed more wheat every year since 1930 than the former government did in the last year they were in power; that
Supply-Trade*-Grain Act

was the crop of 1929-30. At that time if the former government or anybody else had undertaken to interfere with the marketing of wheat, the wheat pools and all the grain companies would have been down upon them like a ton of bricks; they would absolutely have refused to allow the government to have anything to do with the marketing of wheat, and it was under those circumstances the former Minister of Trade and Commerce made the statement he did. It has been entirely unfair for hon. members opposite to make the taunt as they have so frequently done in regard to the words that were used by the former Minister of Trade and Commerce. Now the present Minister of Trade and Commerce says that the marketing of wheat does not come under his department or under any department of government. It is true that a different situation prevails now from that which prevailed when the crop of 1929 was being handled, but it was not until about February, 1930, that the marketing of wheat began to assume a serious aspect. It was at that time the former Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) made the statement he did. I call attention to this because it is an entirely unfair charge against Mr. Malcolm, and I think the situation should 'be understood 'by the committee.

I want to clear this up. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said that neither his department nor any department of the government had anything to do with the marketing of wheat. If they have nothing to do with the marketing of wheat why was the government sending a commissioner to Rome to set a quota? Why did they go to London and set a quota? Why are they interfering at all with the marketing of wheat? How much did all this cost the government, or why was it done, if they had nothing to do with the marketing of wheat?

The hon. gentleman has put a very narrow construction on what I said. The government of Canada, representing the people of Canada, is very much interested in the marketing of the wheat crop. Furthermore the government of this country has placed the credit of the country behind the wheat growers. Is the hon. member opposed to that?

I shall answer it when
the time comes. I am asking the minister a question now.

As far as
the Department of Trade and Commerce is concerned, under the administration of the

Canada Grain Act we are not in the business of marketing wheat but we are in the business of warehousing, grading and whatever is provided for under the Canada Grain Act.

It is rather regrettable that this discussion about the marketing of wheat has come up. Whether the minister likes it or not, whether any department of the government is responsible for the marketing of wheat or not, power was given by this government to a body already in existence to market the wheat of Canada.

No, that
is not a correct statement.

Oh, but it was. You
are operating to-day under the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited, and the power was given by this government to that body to operate. I think it was pretty cute, if I may say so, for the government to give that function to that body and leave no department of government responsible to parliament. There have been only two occasions on which we might deal with the whole matter, and one of them is past. That one was when the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) the other day was putting through the relief bill, under which John I. McFarland operates, and it went right through from resolution to third reading.

Your are operating now for another year under the authority you have operated on up to now. Why should the government subject itsef to the criticism which will be levelled at it when it asks that this grain board be set up?

The Minister of Labour and the government are satisfied with what happened the other day when he put through that, relief legislation. I will wager with the minister now that this grain board bill will never come up, because you are not going to reveal your hand. I was one of those, as I told the minister when he was putting through his relief legislation, who believed up to this time that it might not be in the interests of the grower to make the position public. But what right has this government to ask the people of Canada for a vote of confidence with no knowledge of what has happened through the activities of John I. McFarland? I know the Minister of Trade and Commerce cannot give it; I do not think it is fair to ask him. When he says no department of government is responsible he is right, and that is what I object to. There is no possible way in which we can get at the operations of John I. McFarland in wheat unless it is through the Department of External Affairs headed by the Prime Minister.

No, the
hon. gentleman is wrong, if he will allow me. In the first place his statement that this government has authorized the wheat selling agency is fundamentally wrong.
Tell us what you said.

If you
will refer to the evidence given before the banking committee last year, a statement was there made by John I. McFarland which I understand has never been challenged, that he was asked by the directorate of the wheat selling agency to accept the position which he did accept and still occupies. That agency of course could not carry on the operations which he is and has been carrying on without some backing from the country's credit, and it was got through the relief act. That is where the matter to which hon. gentlemen are referring ought to be discussed. As to whether the information should be made available to the public at this time, I hold the opinion the hon. member for South Battle-ford (Mr. Vallance) held about a year ago in the banking and commerce committee. The hon. gentleman said he would not take the responsibility of revealing to the public just what the commitments were, in view of what was taking place outside of Canada.
I said it here.

And the
position has not been altered.
Oh yes, it has.
Not materially. We shall have to agree to disagree about that. I do not understand that it has been altered. There may be a difference in degree, but I doubt that.
Does the minister believe that it is fair to the people of Canada to ask them to vote confidence in the present government without a knowledge of what the operations of John I. McFarland amount to?
Yes, I think so. I think the people of western Canada who have been reaping the benefits of Mr. McFarland's operations-*
If any.

I do not think there are two opinions among the growers there as far as I have heard. Those people will vote confidence in the government because of the operations of John I. McFarland. It is my view that this discussion is entirely out of order under this item.
So do I. I entirely agree with the minister.

I have risen now for the thirteenth time, and I hope that by so doing I shall not elicit an unlucky answer from the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I wish to vary the question asked by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) in regard to strikes of farmers in Alberta. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is no doubt aware that there was a strike there that lasted through November and December in the vicinity of Mundare, Two Hills, Smokey Lake, Lanuke, St. Paul, Lake Bellevue, Kaleland, Vilna, Beilis, Edward, Rich Valley and Hoad-ley. The grievances were concerned with (1), dockage; (2), grading; (3), installation of cleaners in elevators, and (4), a price commensurate with the cost of production. As the fourth item does not come within the purview of the board of grain commissioners I do not think it fair to ask the minister to make a statement thereon, but so far as the other three items are concerned I would ask the minister what stand the Department of Trade and Commerce has taken on this and also what the stand of the board of grain commissioners is with respect to these matters. I also know that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has received communications from
Supply-Trade-Grain Act

certain bodies in that district in regard to the spread between certain grades of wheat as well as the spread between street prices and spot prices, which more accurately represent the true value of the grain. Furthermore it was resolved that legislation should be enacted at the next session of parliament to enable the board of grain commissioners to investigate, and to regulate in the interests of the producer, all matters relating to grain marketing in western Canada. I do not know whether or not the board of grain commissioners have the necessary powers to investigate these matters or, if they have not, whether the minister intends to give those powers to the board, but I should like the minister to make a statement in that regard.

In regard to the last question, the matter of spreads is outside the jurisdiction of the grain commission at the present moment, but they have filed with the royal commission which is now considering its report-which we hope will be brought in very soon-a brief on the whole subject which makes plain their attitude in regard to this matter. I have not had the privilege of reading that brief, so I cannot speak of its contents, but this is a matter that was referred to the royal commission as being within the purview of its inquiry. I do not know whether or not they will make a recommendation on it; we will have to wait and see.
With regard to the strikes that took place in the hon. gentleman's constituency, correspondence has passed between the hon. gentleman and myself, and a statement has been prepared which I desire to place on record for his benefit and the benefit of members of the house generally.
In November, 1934, the board of grain commissioners received complaints from a number of shipping points in northern Alberta, including Mundare, in regard to the marketing of the crop of that year. The complaints had to do with four different matters: first, dockage; second, grading; third, installation of cleaners in country elevators, and fourth, a price commensurate with the cost of production. The last complaint, namely a price commensurate with the cost of production, was clearly outside the jurisdiction of the board, but in order to be fully informed the board held a number of meetings throughout the area affected.
The situation at Mundare appeared to be the most critical; the complaints had assumed the form of a strike in which certain farmers had agreed not to deliver their grain to the elevators at Mundare or other shipping points. They also are said to have picketed the roads
TMr. Luehkovich.]
to prevent other farmers from delivering their grain. The board decided to make a thorough investigation of the situation at Mundare. A cut-off was made at the same time in each of the eight elevators at that point Inspection officials were sent in to grade the stocks in store. The investigation revealed that only in one instance did the grade of the elevator agent agree with the grade of the board's inspectors. In all other instances the agents of the elevator companies had over-graded; that is to say they had given the grain a higher grade than in the opinion of the board's inspector it was entitled to receive. If the grain had been shipped as of November 15 the companies would have stood to lose approximately S3,200. As a result of the investigation the board could come to no other conclusion than that the complaint at Mundare with respect to grading was not well founded.
In regard to the demand of the farmers that country elevators be required to instal grain cleaners, after assembling all the information available the board came to the conclusion that in northern Alberta at the present time the dockage in grain is of such a character that it would not be economical for the farmers to pay a reasonable charge for cleaning. At a later date the board presented its finding at a public meeting at Mundare, to a large number of farmers and others, and in a short time the strike was lifted and marketing conditions became normal.

I wish to bring to the attention of the minister a matter of a different nature which, strictly speaking, possibly should not be considered as coming under this item. It should have been taken up under the vote for the research council, but it so happened that that vote slipped through here one evening, because of the enthusiastic speed of the official opposition, and some of us did not get a chance to discuss it.
You must have been asleep.

I said "enthusiastic speed", which is not disparaging. Perhaps the matter I am going to bring up will have a soothing effect on the official opposition; it is the question of using wheat to make alcohol. After all the turbulence we have witnessed perhaps this is a good time to bring in this matter for the good effect it may have.
Speak for yourself.

There is a great deal of wheat in store at the present time; in fact our surplus is becoming rather alarming in

Supply-Trade-Grain Act
quantity, and of course the west keeps on producing wheat, so that people are led to cast about for various ways of taking care of this surplus. I know the best way is to sell it and ^hip it overseas, but in recent years markets have not been available, and during the past few years the price of wheat has been very low, so perhaps this is an opportune time to raise this question, and with the minister's consent I will endeavour to place some facts before the committee.
There is a very great deal of gasoline used in Canada for motor fuel purposes. According to my information, based on statistics for 1932 and 1934, approximately 500,000,000 gallons of gasoline are used in Canada every year. Practically all the raw material used for making that refined gasoline is imported. In 1934 we imported crude and partially refined petroleum oil to the extent of 1,063,539,693 gallons, at a cost of over $25,000,000. That amount of money went out of the country, chiefly to the United States, Colombia, Dutch West Indies, Peru, Venezuela and Trinidad. The first cost, of course, went to these various countries, while a small share, amounting to a little over $300,000, went to our government in duty. In addition, in that year there were 15,108,093 gallons of refined gasoline imported, at a total cost of $1,706,796, coming chiefly from the United States and Dutch West Indies. So- it will be seen that there have been large expenditures for motor fuel purposes, most of the money going outside Canada, and in addition in 1934 we had to import tetraethyl lead, which is mixed with gasoline to do away with what are referred to as the knocking qualities in gasoline. We imported 1,398,928 pounds of tetraethyl lead, at a cost of over $1,000,000; this came entirely from the United States. In 1934, therefore, we paid out to other countries something over $27,000,000, in addition to $793,000 in duties to this government, or a total of over $28,000,000 for this purpose.
I am giving these figures, Mr. Chairman, to show what large sums of money go out of our own country in order to supply us with our gasoline requirements. The question of making alcohol from wheat has been investigated very thoroughly. I have here a report of the national research council dated May, 1934, in which they give a detailed account of their investigations in connection with this matter. They tell us that one bushel of wheat will produce approximately two gallons of alcohol. Their proposal as outlined in this report is that we could very well use a ten per cent mixture of alcohol with our gasoline. That would mean ten per cent of
500.000.000 gallons, or 50,000,000 gallons of
alcohol which might very well be mixed with our gasoline for motor fuel purposes. To produce that 50,000,000 gallons of absolute alcohol would require 25,000,000 bushels of wheat. Now if it can be shown that that alcohol can be produced at a cost that is not too exorbitant, it will perhaps appeal to us that it would be something at least worth trying.
This gentleman who operates under the national research council has given us the conversion cost, that is the cost of converting wheat into alcohol, and he takes care to include every little detail. In the first item he has overhead, depreciation, taxes and return on investment, and the cost per gallon under that item is 4.5 cents. The second item is operating charges, labour, fuel, water, chemicals, barley, and so on; that comes to 6.5 cents; dehydrating and denaturing 2 cents. The total cost is 13 cents per gallon. You will notice that he takes in every detail, even allowing for a return on -the investment, and of course we know that in recent years a great many concerns have been carrying on without any return at all on their investment. He also points out that in a large plant, and under favourable conditions, this cost of 13 cents per gallon might be reduced by two or three cents. He points out that no allowance has been made for by-products such as yeast or carbon dioxide, which if sold would reduce that cost of 13 cents.
Now take the matter of wheat prices. In recent years the price of wheat has been very low, and that is what opens up the thought that we might use wheat to advantage-for this purpose. From the bulletin I have here I find that over the four years, 1931, 1932, 1933. 1934, the average price of wheat in Saskatchewan and Alberta was as follows:

So we see that the price of wheat has been extremely low in those four years. The research council has taken the three years, 1930, 1931 and 1932, and they have given us the average price in those years of No. 1 northern and No. 5 wheat. The price of No. 5 in 1930 averaged 51 cents; 1931, 46 cents; 1932, 39 cents. They point out that No. 5 wheat is very useful for the making of alcohol; in fact, it does not need to be a high grade wheat. The lower grade wheat serves fairly well, while it does not produce as much alcohol per bushel. I think it would be fair to assume

that the average price of No. 5 wheat would be 50 cents a bushel in view of what prices have been over the past few years. We find that in the province of Manitoba the use of alcohol in the way suggested a ten per cent mixture, would increase the price of motor fuel by 2.7 cents per gallon; in Saskatchewan it would increase the price by 2.5 cents per gallon, and in Alberta by 3 cents per gallon. They point out that the domestic freight rates are so high for wheat moving to British Columbia that it might be cheaper to manufacture the alcohol in Alberta and ship it to British Columbia, and so they do not give us any price for that province. In Ontario, allowing for the shipping of the wheat from the west to the east, the increase in price would be 3.9 cents per gallon, and in Quebec and the maritimes it would be practically the same. Taking the average for the various provinces we find that the increase in price would be about 3 cents per gallon for a motor fuel with a ten per cent mixture of alcohol added to the gasoline. Let us take that figure and consider what it would mean spread over the whole dominion. In British Columbia it would mean an increased cost to the purchasers of motor fuel of $1,170,000; in Alberta, an increase of $902,000; in Saskatchewan, an increase of $714,000; in Manitoba, an increase of $700,000; in Ontario an increase of $8,260,000; in Quebec, $3,276,000; in the maritimes, $1,260,000. So that the total increase in the cost of the total quantity of gasoline consumed in one year would foe $16,282,000. That may look like a large sum of money to put upon the shoulders of the users of motor fuel, but when we remember that approximately half of that $16,000,000 odd goes into the pockets of the farmers of Canada and the balance into lake and rail freight, elevator charges, manufacturing costs, freight on alcohol, and so on, it does not look so terribly extravagant, because a few minutes ago we pointed out that over $28,000,000 was being sent outside the country for the purpose of supplying us with our motor fuel.
I want to give some of the benefits that would come from a mixture of alcohol with our gasoline. Perhaps one of the most important benefits is obtained from the antiknock qualities of gasoline when mixed with alcohol. That is the reason that refiners of gasoline have to import tetraethyl lead to mix with gasoline to eliminate the knocking properties which gasoline naturally has. By mixing absolute alcohol with the gasoline it is not necessary to use tetraethyl lead. In fact, we are told by these research men 
that the use of alcohol has a better effect on the gasoline than the use of tetraethyl lead.
Another advantage would be that it would reduce the formation of carbon in the engine, reduce the oil consumption of the engine, and give a longer life to the valves and the engine parts in general due to the smoother operation. While we have no absolute figures or estimates on these points, that is the conclusion of the research council as to the effect of mixing alcohol with gasoline. Also, Mr. Chairman, it would reduce our imports considerably, thus helping our trade balance. Another important point in its favour is that it would tend to give an impetus to the distilling business in Canada. In 1933 we had eighteen distilleries in Canada, which produced a little over 3,500,000 gallons of absolute alcohol.
I do not wish to interfere with the hon. member's remarks, but unless he has the consent of the committee he is certainly out of order.

I agree,
Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member's remarks are out of order, but he was good enough to write me a letter saying that he intended bringing this matter up. I have no objection, and with the consent of the committee I would ask that he be allowed to proceed.

I have no objection
to the hon. member proceeding, but I hope the minister will show the same courtesy to the rest of the members.
I shall be courteous to everyone.
The minister is very good natured and I thank him for it.

It is not only the minister
who is good natured. Before the hon. member proceeds I think he owes hon. gentlemen on this side an apology, as he can proceed only with their consent. We shall be glad to make the consent unanimous if an apology is forthcoming.

I shall be glad to accommodate the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff). I am ready to apologize or do anything else in order to keep going.
I was referring to the good effects which might be expected to accrue from the use of alcohol in gasoline, and the last one I mentioned was the benefit which the distilling business would gain. We have eighteen distilleries which produced 3,500,000 gallons in

1933, and if provision were made for the production of 50,000,000 gallons, there would be a great impetus to the business as well as an increased pay-roll. There would also be provided a new domestic market for 25,000,000 bushels of wheat as well as for a considerable quantity of barley.
There is another important point to be kept in mind. We are told that the reserves of gasoline are not inexhaustible and that as they gradually decrease there would be a rise in the price of gasoline. Some authorities predict that this will come about within the next ten years. I should like to give certain facts in connection with other countries. At the present time England is erecting a plant for the hydrogenation of coal to produce gasoline for fuel. It is expected that 30,000,000 gallons per year will be produced. This fuel will cost from 16 to 18 cents per gallon while gasoline costs only six cents per gallon delivered in British ports. In order to assist the coal industry the British government is bonusing this hydrogenation process to the extent of eight cents per gallon. This will encourage the use of British coal to produce a fuel within the country rather than to be dependent upon imports.
There are eleven countries in which motor fuel containing alcohol is being marketed. Germany is making alcohol from potatoes and molasses and mixing it with her motor fuel. France is making it from cane and beet molasses while Italy is making it from molasses and grapes. Sweden is producing alcohol from sulphite liquor; Czechoslovakia is producing it from potatoes and molasses; the Philippines use molasses in this process while Latvia uses potatoes. Australia, Cuba and South Africa use molasses in the process. Hungary is producing alcohol but I have not the product they use. The use of alcohol varies from ten to twenty-five per cent. There are several other countries considering the use of alcohol in their motor fuel, such as Brazil, Chile, Austria, Equador, Poland and the United States. The products to be used include molasses, potatoes and corn. India and the Irish Free State are providing government assistance for the production of motor alcohol.
Having placed these facts before the committee, the minister and the government- and for that matter the official opposition, who hope in tihe not distant future to be returned to power-I should like to suggest that this matter be considered and carried beyond the experimental work being done by the national research council. This council has done excellent work in bringing these facts before the public and I commend to any hon. member who may be interested the reading of this
book. I suggest that a further step be taken and that alcohol be manufactured on a larger scale. Perhaps this may not be done to the extent of producing 50,000,000 gallons, but 1 think it should be tried out in order to test the facts brought out by the research council. If the advantages are such as are pointed out in this book it may be that none of us would object to paying three cents more per gallon for our gasoline when we obtain a fuel of a superior quality. When the refineries commenced using tetraethyl in their gasoline they charged the customer two cents per gallon extra because of its superior quality. If the mixing of alcohol will provide a fuel of a superior quality, an extra charge of three cents per gallon will not be of much importance. 1 thank the minister and the committee for giving me the opportunity of placing these facts before them.

Mr. Chairman, I shall not detain the committee very long in continuing this discussion. As I am reminded by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff), it has often been said that gasoline and alcohol do not mix. However, we are not using that statement in the same sense as the hon. member for Kin-dersley (Mr. Carmichael). This whole matter was the subject of an investigation by the national research council and a memorandum has been prepared on the possible utilization of grain alcohol in motor fuel in Canada. The first finding was that the manufacture of alcohol from wheat offers no technical difficulty. Second, they found that the use of such alcohol in admixture with gasoline for motor fuel is technically possible, as demonstrated by its continued sale for this purpose in France, Germany and other countries. Third, alcohol cannot be made as cheaply as gasoline by any process known at the present time. For this reason the blending of alcohol with gasoline is bound to increase the cost of .motor fuel. Four, other things being equal, the addition of ten per cent of alcohol would be expected to increase the cost of motor fuel by at least three cents per gallon on an average for all Canada. This figure is based on the use of No. 5 wheat at a price of sixty cents per bushel at Fort William, approximately the present price. About 25,000,000 bushels of wheat would be required annually. Five, the addition of alcohol to gasoline improves the anti-knock qualities and lessens carbon formation. These advantages are partly offset by certain unfavourable characteristics. Six, in order to produce the alcohol required for a ten per cent blend, it would be necessary to increase the capacity of the
Supply-Trade-Grain Act

distilling industry. Seven, it is believed that motor fuel made by the hydrogenation of Canadian coal would be considerably cheaper than motor alcohol made from wheat costing sixty cents per bushel. I shall be glad to direct the attention of the officials of the research council to the speech of the hon. member for Ivindersley and ask them to look into the matter with a view to having further investigations made.
Is it not true that cars in which alcohol is used go faster than those using gasoline?
I am not an expert and I do not know.

The hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Vallance) referred to the activities of Mr. John I. McFarland and this government in the wheat market. I desire to ask the minister if he will assure the committee that an opportunity will be given before the end of the session to discuss the activities of Mr. McFarland and the government in the wheat market. If the minister can give us that assurance I shall content myself with correcting just one statement which he made. The minister stated a while ago that all that this government did was to guarantee the account of Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited at the bank and had nothing whatever to do with sustaining the market or with speculating or gambling in wheat. I want to show him that that statement is wrong when viewed in the light of a statement made by the former Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens). On March 28, 1933, the former minister, when dealing with this matter, said that he recognized this fact but appreciating the loss which would be entailed, particularly to the producer, the government authorized John I. McFarland to purchase grain for future deliveries. I understood the minister to say that the government had not authorized John I. McFarland, that it was the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers Limited that authorized him. But the former Minister of Trade and Commerce states definitely that it was the government that authorized him.

I do not understand that statement to be correct; I understand the statement to be correct which I made, that Mr. McFarland was appointed by the selling agency and that all that this government did as such was to pass an order in council under the relief act guaranteeing the banks against ultimate loss through his operations.

I am giving the words
of the former Minister of Trade and Commerce.

I do not
understand it in that light.

I cannot read it in
any other light. What does the minister say now in regard to the possibility of discussing the activities of John I. McFarland?

I have
every reason to believe that the resolution standing in the name of the Prime Minister will be proceeded with, and when that is done there will be ample opportunity to discuss the whole question. The present intention of the government is to proceed with that bill.
If it is not proceeded with will the minister assure us that we shall have an opportunity to discuss the subject?

I cannot
give that assurance. The proper place to have discussed this whole question-and I believe it was discussed-was under the relief act, because technically this whole question comes under the relief legislation.
The minister will remember that for three or four years we have discussed under this very item the activities of the government and of John I. McFarland..

I am not
aware of that, but I take the hon. member's word for it without any verification because he has been in the past much more interested in the subject than I have been. But technically the proper place to have discussed the item was under the relief act.

I agree with the minister that possibly this is not the proper time to discuss the subject, but as the hon. member for Willow Bunch has pointed out, it was discussed in 1932 in connection with the estimates. I have here volume 2 of the session of 1932, and on April 15 you will find at pages 2078-9 and elsewhere trade and commerce supply, and the whole question was then under discussion. I will read a few extracts:
Mr. Young: Last year the government gave a guarantee of a minimum price of wheat. Has the minister any statement to make to the committee as to how the government stands now as a result of that guarantee?

That in
itself was not a quite correct statement. There never was any other guarantee given, except that against ultimate loss.

The minister's predecessor took the same position that he does, but only up to a certain point. Let me quote his reply to the hon. member for Weyburn:
Mr. Stevens:	There was no government
guarantee of the price of wheat. My hon. friend is perhaps giving a wrong impression.
I quote that to show that a discussion did take place. .Now John I. McFarland is to-day performing a dual function, both as head of the sales agency of the pools and as stabilizer for this government, and1 it is the stabilization effort of John I. McFarland that we want to get at. When the minister says that we should have discussed the subject under the relief measure, I think he is right. But we had an assurance from his colleague the Minister of Labour, because of the position I pointed out, that one of two men should be on the floor of the house, *either the Prime Minister, who we are sorry is not able to be here, or John I. McFarland; and because neither of them was here -Mr. McFarland was not sitting in front of the minister, and the Prime Minister was absent-the Minister of Labour was asked for the assurance which the hon. member for Willow Bunch has requested again, that the resolution now standing in the name of the Prime Minister would be proceeded with for the setting up of a grain board. And the Minister of Labour assured us that it would. If the Minister of Trade and Commerce gives us the same assurance, I am absolutely in agreement with him that the proper time to discuss the subject is when you are setting up a grain board, inasmuch as Mr. McFarland's activities cannot continue if a grain board is set up. But that is why I make the statement that a grain board will never be set up, because we have the assurance in connection with the relief act that John I. McFarland may operate for another year.

I have
no doubt that the opening statement of the hon. gentleman is correct, that this subject has previously been discussed under this item; I have not the slightest doubt that the discussion did take place. But on that point I can only reaffirm the position I have already taken, that any discussion of this matter was not germane to the inquiry, though I never raised that as an objection. With respect to the assurance which hon. gentlemen have asked me to give, I can only repeat that it is the government's policy to proceed with the resolution standing in the name of the Prime Minister for the formation of a grain board, and ample
opportunity will be given when that is reached to discuss the whole question. That is the position I take, and I can give no positive assurance. But I know of no other line of policy on the part of the government, and I am not prepared to say that any consideration has been given any other course.
Mr. VALLANiCE:	To-day, on the orders
of the day, I asked the acting leader of the government when we might expect the resolution now standing in the name of the Prime Minister to come before the house, and we got the same evasive reply which we have now received from the minister. I realize the minister's position; he is only administering a department of government. But we did expect that the leader of the government would give us some assurance to-day in reply to the question put to him. I have nothing further to say.

The resolution standing in the name of the Prime Minister has not been proceeded with on account of his absence; that is the reason and nothing else. It is hoped that the Prime Minister will be in a position to take care of the matter himself before prorogation. That is the hope of the government.

I am prompted to say another word. If you glance at the order paper you will see that there are two or three items standing in the name of the Prime Minister. Two have been proceeded with by other ministers, and I think that the acting Prime Minister should be in a position to give us an assurance, in view of the fact that the other two pieces of legislation standing in the name of the Prime Minister have already been proceeded with, that possibly some other minister may proceed with the resolution on which it proposed to base a bill for the establishment of a grain board.

Because other items standing in the name of the Prime Minister have been proceeded with by other ministers, it does not follow that this will or will not; I do not think there is any relation between the two. But it is desirable that the Prime Minister should proceed with this, and that is the hope and expectation of the government.

This item calls for $1.900,000. I understand that a charge is made for each bushel of grain handled under the act; and in the budget, in the list of non-tax revenues, there are items each year roughly corresponding to the amount of this vote.
Supply-Trade-Grain Act

How much per bushel does the government charge under this act? Is it enough to cover the administration? Is there a surplus or a deficit?

The charge is $1 a thousand bushels for inspection and $1 a thousand bushels for weighing, and in a good year there is a little credit balance ; in a poor year it is the other way. Generally speaking the charges take care of the operation of the act. I could give the hon. gentleman the exact figures for the year if he desires them, but they all appear in the public accounts for previous years and we have the latest figures.

May I ask the minister a question1 with regard to garnet wheat? As I came in I thought I heard him say that there was a possibility of the legislation passed last year not being put into operation for this year.
I do not think I said that there was a possibility.

I would like to get exactly what the minister said.
Mr. HANiSON (York-Sunbury): I said that the government's intention at present was to let the legislation go into effect, but that representations had 'been made with respect to holding up the operation of the act for a period of time, and the question is now really being considered by the government. None of the reasons which occasioned a change in the statute last year has altered. The present consideration has been given because I am advised by the board of grain commissioners that in the event of considerable quantities of No. 2 northern wheat being in store on July 31, the quantity being wholly problematical, considerable difficulty will be occasioned by this fact. It is therefore on the grounds of expediency only that the postponement of last year's legislation is even being considered. There is in this year's estimates an item of $75,000 which is intended to finance the shipment of commercial quantities of garnet wheat in an effort to establish the commercial spread of pure garnet with the regular class grades. At the moment I am not able to say that a decision has been reached one way or the other with respect to garnet. We do not think we have to make a decision now, but if it is decided not to do anything, of course the act will automatically come into operation on the first day of August next. If it is decided to do anything, due notice will be given.

The reason I bring this question up is that in the west spring will probably break in about two weeks.- The western farmers have been led to believe it will ibe wise for them on account of the legislation passed last year to get into some other wheat, but if that legislation is not going to come into operation, many of them would like to get garnet seed wheat as soon as they can.

Regulations were passed in Saskatchewan and Alberta under which no chickens could be imported from British Columbia or elsewhere unless the poultry flocks had been tested for B.W.D. I think that comes under the health of animals branch.
Under live stock.

In Saskatchewan and Alberta the veterinaries recommended what is known as the long test; I think the minister understands what I mean. That has caused a great deal of misgiving among the poultry men of British Columbia. In British Columbia they have been experimenting to a considerable extent with both tests, and while it is true that the dominion government provided financial assistance this spring so that the poultry men of the province might have their poultry flocks tested free of charge by the long test method, the fact remains that this question so far as our province is concerned is very much in doubt.
May I point out to the minister that the poultry men of British Columbia have made many tests in the matter, and while there is no infallible test for pullorum disease-I think that is generally agreed-if the method that has been adopted and pursued by Saskatchewan and Alberta, and approved by the federal department, is carried out it will mean an excessive financial burden on the poultry men
of British Columbia. By the quick test method the poultry man can make the test himself and tell in a short time whether his poultry have pullorum disease or not, but if he is going to be compelled to carry out the regulations laid down by Saskatchewan and Alberta it will mean a cost to him of between six and seven cents per head of poultry. Not only that but Saskatchewan and Alberta do not go into poultry raising so extensively as British Columbia, and in Saskatchewan and A-lberta the regulations provide that the whole flock must be tested. Such a regulation would work a great hardship with us because the average poultry man with a flock of one or two thousand head may have a breeding pen of only six hundred or so, and if he is compelled to comply with the regulations laid down by Saskatchewan and Alberta and approved by the federal department he will be out six or seven cents per head of poultry for every chicken on his place.
I am going to urge upon the minister that the whole matter be reviewed. I know that the veterinaries will contend that their method is the best, but as a poultry man and from the information that has been given to me I can say that neither of the two tests is infallible. Y ou can test a chicken to-day for that disease and get a clear test, and tomorrow the chicken may have the disease. There is no infallible test. I think I am about correct in saying that it is impossible to tell which is the better method. One is just as good as the other. I appeal to the minister on behalf of the poultry men of our province who have now to comply with the conditions laid down by Saskatchewan and Alberta, and laid down, I think I am safe in saying, to prevent the selling in Alberta and Saskatchewan of day old chicles from British Columbia. Their regulations were engineered, I believe, by some hatchery men in Saskatchewan and Alberta, helped out by the veterinaries of the department. These regulations are aimed principally against British Columbia. British Columbia, of course, is carrying on just now under a provincial and a dominion policy, and they are carrying on this past season because they have been helped financially. We do not know what policy will be adopted next year, but if the1 health of animals branch insist that the test must be carried out as laid down by the veterinaries, it will mean a cost of six or seven cents per head of poultry to the poultry men of British Columbia. The authorities who have done most work in various countries are of the opinion that so far it is the most accurate test that has been discovered. Other tests have been used, but the tube test method has proved the most reliable. The test referred to by the two hon. gentlemen who have spoken is in the experimental stage. It has not yet been accepted as being as accurate as the test I have mentioned. There is nothing that the department would rather do than adopt the test to which they referred as soon as it has been verified, although we have had no complaints from any of the poultry breeders in British Columbia against the test that is being used there. It is not necessary for them to use that test unless they wish to trade with, other provinces. The whole matter is this. The different provinces asked for a uniform test, and the authorities in the best position to

advise did advise that the most accurate test was the one that is being used. The other is in the experimental stage and as soon as it is admitted that it is as accurate as the test I have discussed, and the cheapness of it is established, it will be, I should say, favourably considered.

Did the minister say he

As to the effect
on the birds. Comparatively recently a committee of the poultry breeders in British Columbia have sat in with their minister of agriculture and agreed on this method that is being followed at the present time. I can assure hon. gentlemen that very careful consideration will be given the statements they have made in this connection.

In view of the large number of horses killed' in the eastern townships last year, supposed to have been affected by glanders, has the minister had any further investigation made, and has he any statement on the matter?

A very full investigation has been made with regard to horses tested for glanders. As soon as it was discovered that glanders existed, the most experienced veterinaries in the service were sent to the area to deal with this outbreak. Colonel Tamblyn was sent to the district and performed a number of post mortem examinations along with other veterinaries who wished to be present to demonstrate beyond doubt that it was glanders. Others asked for post mortem examinations, but in this disease there is danger unless the examination is carried out with the greatest care. I think what the hon. member has in mind is that some of the horses tested, that were suspicious, were not destroyed, while other horses that were tested, and did react, were destroyed. It was within the option of the owner of a horse, if it was tested and reacted for glanders, to request that it be not destroyed, and if he could give an assurance that that horse would be kept in (absolute isolation for further tests, the department if it could satisfy itself that the undertaking would be lived up to without danger of the disease being spread, would quarantine the horse for further tests.
A request has come and a test will be proceeded with.

This was the appropriation on which the minister was going tc give us an explanation of the policy of the government with respect to the drought areas in the western provinces. Possibly he would like to elaborate what 'he has already said and thus dispense with a number of questions that would otherwise be necessary. I should be very glad to hear him disclose his policy. I have before me some newspaper clippings taken from such a reliable authority as the Toronto Mail and Empire, which should be good enough for a good Conservative, indicating the intention of making a sort of crown colony of that western country, taking over the whole thing. We do not want to be hypercritical about how the assistance is to be given, but it occurs to some of us that some sort of cooperation between the federal and provincial governments might be practised to advantage in carrying on this tremendous work, because it is a tremendous task.

The appropriation now under discussion, that is experimental farms, does not include the money for this work that is contemplated and that is to commence almost immediately now in connection with the drought areas in the three prairie provinces. So far as many newspaper reports are concerned, I think the hon. member for Melville has perhaps had somewhat the same experience that I have had, that one reads more in the press about what is going on in one's department than either the officials or the minister himself could have any idea is supposed to be going on. There is no thought in the mind of the federal Department of Agriculture of changing its policy

of cooperation with any provincial department of agriculture. This is really an extension of survey work that has taken place during the past two or three years and a continuation of undertakings that were started in 1927 as a result of the work commenced at the Manyberries station. Illustration stations have been set up in increasing numbers throughout this area to deal with various small districts as one farm, but it was felt, because of the smallness of that experiment and the undue effect of local conditions, the work should be extended to include larger areas. It was decided with the cooperation of the farmers on the land to increase the number from twenty-one to forty-one. In addition to that there will be new areas in cooperation with the farmers of two sections. Besides that, it is contemplated to set up five townships of thirty-six square miles each one in Alberta, three in Saskatchewan and one in Manitoba. Some of those will be used in an endeavour to demonstrate that even with a continuation of the drought, results even better in many cases than under present conditions can be achieved. The first aim is to demonstrate, in conjunction with what knowledge we already have, whether or not if the drought continues farmers can by certain practices do more towards obtaining a livelihood than they are doing at the present time. I believe that there are many farmers in the drought area who if they had sufficient capital

for their capital has been drained over a period of years-could have available at all times seed such as fall rye or sweet clover or grasses so that when there are rains throughout the summer after the wheat is put in they could seed some land with these grasses and have at least some feed for the winter. It is to demonstrate some of those things that these experiments are being conducted; also how far we should use the strip farming system. I may say this for the -information of hon. members, especially those from the west, that for the last two or three years in these- illustration stations the cultural practices adopted have shown better results than those obtained by the average farmer -in the neighbourhood. It is true these stations have been selected with considerable care and it is not altogether fair to compare work done in them with the work done by the average farmer in the same neighbourhood. In addition to illustration stations, outstanding farmers will be assisted financially in this connection in carrying out some of their own ideas under supervision. Where it is felt that conditions are suitable,

some townships will be used for the planting of trees, because there are instances even- in almost the centre of the drought areas where certain farmers believe they have obtained better results by the use of shelter belts not only around the buildings but fairly extensive belts throughout the farm. This supervised work will take in almost all conditions in the west, on areas of greater size than the smaller illustration farms. In addition we also purpose undertaking investigational and demonstration work in areas th-at have- been abandoned entirely, for the purpose of seeing what can be done to reclaim them. Furthermore a survey has been made, and I believe last year close to a thousand applications were made at Manyberries station alone to Mr. Thompson, the officer in charge, for expert advice and assistance- with reference to the making of small dams to obtain a larger supply of water. These may be just mud dams with a small spillway that farmers can build themselves, but they require engineering advice as to where- they should be situated. Then there is also need for larger dams costing from $10,000 up to $15,000. By holding the freshets in the spring they might assure to farmers or ranchers a supply of hay and green feed for the winter and for a dry year. It was felt that because of the nature of this work and -what has -been done by our federal officers this clean cut program should be set out and put under the- supervision of the experimental farm system. Thus there is no lack of cooperation with the provinces. The same rule will apply in this work as has applied-for it is an extension of work that has been done in the past-that is, a -full measure o-f cooperation.

Then I understand that the system of demonstration plots which was established about twelve or fifteen years ag-o more or less all over Canada has been evolving into these larger plots. For instance, south of Yellow Grass in the burnt-out area there is a plot consisting I think of a half section. North of Piapot near Maple Creek there is another. I think in the last few years a whole section has been devoted to demonstration purposes, trying to overcome some of these terrible difficulties that have prevailed in that area for some- years. The proposal now is to extend these demonstration plots into five larger areas each eighteen miles square, and continue the practice of experimentation and demonstration, including the planting of shelter belts in suitable places, the making of dams, and the digging of reser-

voirs. I have no exception to take to that; but we have always been doing something of that, if not by the Department of Agriculture by the provincial public works or highways departments. Since 1914 a large number of dams and reservoirs in suitable runways have been constructed. This is merely an extension or an evolution of what has been taking place for many years. Does the minister not think that the first thing to do in that country is to try to keep the soil at home? Some of those areas we must admit are unsuitable for tilling; every time you stir the soil with a plough or any other implement it takes wings and off it goes and lands in Ontario or somewhere, just as Oklahoma and Kansas and Colorado, are now sending their dust storms north, so that probably some of our lost prairie land will be restored to us. But I think everyone admits now that some of those areas should not have been cultivated, although in wet years they grow good crops of the highest quality. There is no part of the west that has grown larger and better crops in wet years than that same area. Nevertheless there are some marginal lands, and if we want to keep them at home they must at the earliest opportunity be seeded down, through government support in some form. Two or three years ago the federal Department of Agriculture started out bravely enough distributing small amounts of grass and clover seed, but so far as my information goes very little of that was done in,this dried out area. It should be done1 there, for even if only thinly seeded it wiil soon spread. As a matter of fact there is a large area between Medicine Hat and Brooks that has gone back to grass, has a fine sod on it, better than the pi-airie. But that had not been under tillage very long, consequently it was not difficult to regrass naturally. But as to this area we are talking about, which has been under tillage for a quarter of a century, a lot of it will take a long time to regrass. It will soon get covered with some form of vegetation, however, for nature abhors a vacuum; the Russian thistle will soon cover it and perhaps hold the land from drifting. But something of more value than the Russian thistle should be introduced-grasses and clovers including crested wheat grass which survives the drought better than any other known grass so far. I think the federal government will have to take charge of that and seed down those large areas in cooperation with the prairie provinces, as it is to them these abandoned lands will revert automatically.
I do not know whether or not the minister contemplates establishing what we call district representatives. I recall that back in 1914, when the first tremendous drought struck that area, the dominion government of the day became quite anxious and established district representatives without consulting the provinces at all, so we had two sets of these officers, one representing the federal and the other the provincial government. I submit that that should be avoided as far as possible, and I am sure the minister knows the enormity of that undertaking. If there is any way at all, by friendly cooperation with the provinces, of avoiding overlapping, against which the minister has always expressed himself, I hope that will be done. I assume that this abandoned property naturally reverts to the municipalities, because of the unpaid taxes, or else to the provincial government. How does the minister propose to overcome that situation and at the same time seed down these larger provincial or municipal areas which have been found to be unprofitable except in the very best years?

With reference to
the distribution of grasses, the same distribution-and perhaps more so-has been made in the drought area that has been made in the other parts of the province.
Perhaps the minister will tell us how they succeeded?

The difficulty was
that because of the small plots that could be seeded with the grass seed given them, they were blown out, and results were not satisfactory. Perhaps another reason was that they were seeded in the early part of the year, whereas the intention now is to have a supply on hand when moisture does come, and these grasses can be seeded late in the fall or early in the spring. It is not only necessary to have a relatively large supply of seed; we feel that it is necessary to have enough seed so that it can be almost wasted in these localities. It very seldom happens that a plant particularly suited to the drought area is suited to other areas, yet it was necessary to obtain a supply of grass seed, and that was one of the investigations we carried on. Much to our delight it was found that this grass seed suitable in the south in particular also does very well in the north, so much so that it will increase from two pounds to six hundred pounds an acre. The best of that seed has been retained and is being distributed in the north, under very careful supervision to hurry its propagation. Investigation was carried on in connection

I just wanted to make an appeal to the minister. In the section from which I come we have one of the finest experimental farms in the dominion. May I ask the minister how many illustration farms there are in the constituency of Kamouraska at the present time?
I do not think we have the information in that form, but I shall be glad to give it to my hon. friend.
Does the opening of a new experimental farm near the town of Melfort mean the gradual elimination of the Rosthern farm?

No, it will not affect the Rosthern farm in any way. A certain program has been carried on in connection with the Rosthern farm; that is being enlarged and proceeded with. There has been no change in the policy in connection with the Rosthern farm as the result of the establishment of the Melfort farm, nor will there be any such change.

I happened to be up in my hon. friend's area last harvest, and there was a good deal of discussion about the experimental farm at Melfort. Of course all rumours must be discounted a good deal, but at that time it was rumoured that this property had been expropriated without the consent or knowledge of the owners, and that
the two farmers who formerly owned the property knew nothing about it. I do not know that this would be particularly harmful; indeed' if the government thought they were going to miss the opportunity of getting the property that would be the correct thing to do, though of course it is desirable to avoid it if possible. Perhaps the minister will tell us why that particular property was chosen. I understand that it is three or four miles from the town of Melfort and not very accessible to visitors. Perhaps all these matters will be explained to the committee. I should like to know just why that choice was made. I do not suggest there was anything improper about it; so far as I know it is quite suitable, but they seemed to be in a great hurry about it. Temporary stables were rushed up and cattle were sent there just at the beginning of winter, when there was no shelter for them. There seemed to be just a certain amount of time and everything had to be done within that time limit.
I am sure the minister will be able to clear up the situation with a word.

The owners of the farms were negotiated with and it was understood that they were willing to accept certain prices. Then difficulties arose and it was decided that it would be fairer to everyone concerned to make it a matter of expropriation. This farm was selected as being typical of that area. It was not intended that we should have an ideal farm, because an ideal farm would not provide a fair comparison for the problems existing in that district. The farm is situated on the highway and is readily accessible from Melfort. I believe the corner of the farm is about two miles from Melfort. There was no particular rush in connection with the farm; its establishment had been contemplated for some time, for the reason that in this whole area, extending from Dauphin to Lloyd-minister, no farm existed. The conditions in that area are very different from the conditions with which the Rosthern farm has to deal, and for a good many years it was felt that a farm should be established in that area. I believe the hon. member gave that question very serious consideration when he was Minister of Agriculture.

Perhaps the minister will tell us where the foundation live stock that we sent to the Melfort farm came from.
